graders.evidence:
I've read all three reference files. Here's the review.

# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page — testimonial + deployment line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** **Fachkreise** — gated, credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering. HWG § 11 does **not** apply. § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (copy targets Germany; claim references DACH)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 2 verify.

**Ready to publish: With changes below.**

No breach is established on the material in front of me. All three claims rest on facts I haven't seen — an attribution, a measurement, a deployment footprint. That makes this a verification job against the technical file and the customer records, not a rewrite.

**The audience call does most of the work here.** A credentialed-login page restricted to procurement and clinical engineering is Fachkreise on the reference's own list ("clinicians, hospital procurement"). That switches off all of HWG § 11 — including **no. 11 on third-party testimonials**. A named-clinician quote is not a finding on this page. It would be a live question on an ungated page, and even there only if abusive, repulsive or misleading — testimonials are not flatly prohibited for devices. If this page's gating is softer than described (shared logins, a public preview, indexable content), tell me and I'll re-run the § 11 pass.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** An attributed clinician endorsement to Fachkreise engages no prohibition in the verified provisions. § 11 no. 11 is out of scope by audience; § 3 contains no testimonial limb.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent from the clinician and the institution; confirmation of the exact title and affiliation as of publication; the German original of the quote if it was translated; disclosure of any commercial relationship (advisory board, consultancy, research funding, speaker fees).
**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** — if Prof. Ellwanger is or was "für [den Hersteller] tätig", then statements about their "Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge" fall inside 3(b), and an inaccurate title or affiliation becomes a breach. If they are genuinely independent, 3(b) does not reach them at all.
- **UWG § 5(1)** — if the relationship is compensated and the quote is presented as unpaid clinical experience, the presentation is "zur Täuschung geeignet" on a point a procurement reader could decide on.
- **UWG § 5(1)** — "Universitätsklinikum Süd" does not read like a German university hospital's actual name; German Universitätskliniken are named by city. If this is an anonymisation or a composite, presenting it as a specific named institution is an unwahre Angabe. If it's anonymised for confidentiality, say so ("ein Universitätsklinikum in Süddeutschland") rather than inventing a name.

**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** I have no performance data, so I can't say the device lacks this property — and "this might not be substantiated" is a verification item, not an Art. 7(a) breach. But two things on the face of the copy make it expensive to defend: **"every"** is a universal quantifier, and the **baseline is unstated** — two steps out of *what*? The predecessor system, a competitor's system, a manual workflow, an earlier software version? A reader cannot tell, and neither can I.
**Evidence needed:** The measurement behind "two steps" — workflow step counts before and after, the comparator identified, how many registrations, at how many sites, and whether the reduction held across anatomy/approach variation or was specific to this centre's protocol. If it is one clinician's impression rather than a measured count, the copy must say so.
**Also engaged:**
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** and **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") — if the reduction is not measured, or is real at this site but not generalisable, then publishing it as an unqualified product property ascribes a property the device does not have and sets an expected result the buyer won't get.
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** — if the unstated baseline is an identifiable competitor's system and the market can tell who is meant, this is comparative advertising. "Erkennbar" does not require naming. It would then have to be objective and **nachprüfbar** — and an unstated baseline is by definition not checkable from public information. Comparison is lawful in Germany; an unverifiable one is not.

**Call:** Needs substantiation — and reword to attribute it as single-site experience regardless of what the data shows.

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A true deployment statement breaches nothing. Three facts inside it are load-bearing and unverified: the geography ("DACH" asserts all three countries), the character of use ("routine" excludes pilots, evaluations and clinical investigations), and the date.
**Evidence needed:** Installed-base list by country with go-live dates; confirmation that the earliest routine — not pilot — deployment was in 2024; confirmation that the deployed configuration is the certified one.
**Also engaged:**
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("Verfügbarkeit") — if the footprint is DE and AT only, "DACH" is an unwahre Angabe. If some sites are pilots, evaluations or investigation sites, "routine use" is zur Täuschung geeignet. Both are material to a procurement reader assessing deployment maturity.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 4** ("Zulassung der Waren") — the **CH** in DACH is the one to check. Claiming routine Swiss use implies the device is lawfully on the Swiss market. Switzerland is outside the EU and its own requirements are **outside what this skill verifies** — I'm flagging the UWG consequence, not stating the Swiss rule. Confirm Swiss market access with your regulatory team before "DACH" ships.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 4** — if use in 2024 ran under a legacy or narrower certificate, or under a different device version, the line implies a certification history the device may not hold.

**Call:** Verify

---

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU — specifically, whether the IFU conditions registration on a verification or accuracy-check step, since the quote is about removing steps from registration. **I am not raising (c).** I have no IFU, no intended purpose and no risk documentation, and inferring a likely risk from the device category would produce a finding nobody could falsify. Put the IFU in front of me and I'll give you a real answer.

## Considered and not raised

Recording these so you know they were tested, not missed:

- **HWG § 11 no. 11** (testimonials) — not applicable. Audience is Fachkreise.
- **HWG § 11 no. 9** (unrecognisable promotional purpose) — same reason. Also, on a gated vendor page the promotional purpose is self-evident.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** (Erfolg mit Sicherheit) — "every registration" is absolute, but § 3 no. 2(a) targets certainty of *therapeutic* success. A workflow step count is not an Erfolg in that sense. The absoluteness problem is real; its home is UWG § 5(2) no. 1, where I've put it.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** (no harmful effects) — the copy makes no side-effect claim. "Routine use since 2024" is a track record statement, not a safety reassurance.
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only. Never applies to a device.

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

Assumes verification lands; bracketed fields are yours to fill.

**German (market language for a DE page):**

> Prof. [Vorname Nachname], [Fachrichtung], Universitätsklinikum [Stadt]: „In unserem Workflow entfielen zwei Schritte pro Registrierung."
> Einzelzentrum-Erfahrung, Vergleichsbasis: [Vorgängersystem / manueller Workflow]. Nicht ohne Weiteres auf andere Zentren übertragbar. [Prof. [Nachname] ist unabhängig. | Prof. [Nachname] ist für [Hersteller] als [Rolle] tätig.]
> Seit [Monat] 2024 im Routineeinsatz in [n] Kliniken in [Deutschland und Österreich].
> Anwendung gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.

**English equivalent, if the page stays in English:**

> Prof. [Name], [specialty], Universitätsklinikum [City]: "Two steps dropped out of our registration workflow."
> Single-centre experience; baseline: [predecessor system / manual workflow]. Not necessarily transferable to other centres. [Independent. | Prof. [Name] serves as [role] for [manufacturer].]
> In routine use at [n] hospitals in [Germany and Austria] since [month] 2024.
> Use in accordance with the instructions for use.

Four changes, each doing specific work: the **single-centre + baseline** line converts an unverifiable general claim into a narrow, checkable one — narrow and verifiable is cheap to defend, broad and unverifiable is expensive even when true. The **relationship disclosure** closes the § 5(1) exposure. Naming **actual countries** instead of "DACH" closes § 5(2) nos. 1 and 4, and drops the Swiss market-access question entirely. The **IFU pointer** is cheap insurance on limb (c) — I'm not asserting (c) requires it, but it costs one line.

If the page stays in English, keep the German original of the quote on file; a translated quote inside quotation marks has to render faithfully what was actually said.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Attribution | Consent from clinician + institution; exact title/affiliation at publication; German original of the quote | Marketing / Legal |
| Attribution | Disclosure of any commercial relationship with the manufacturer | Medical Affairs / Compliance |
| "Universitätsklinikum Süd" | Confirm the institution's real name, or relabel as anonymised | Marketing |
| "two steps" | Step-count measurement, comparator identified, n registrations, n sites | Clinical / Product |
| "every registration" | Whether the reduction held across anatomy and approach variation | Clinical |
| "DACH" | Installed base by country with go-live dates | Sales Ops |
| "routine use" | Which sites are routine vs pilot / evaluation / investigation | Sales Ops |
| "since 2024" | Earliest routine go-live; certificate scope and version in use at that date | Regulatory |
| Limb (c) | Does the IFU record a likely risk — e.g. a registration verification step? | Regulatory / RA |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | File | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` | [verified] |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(a), 2(b), 3(b) | `references/hwg.md` | [verified] |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 9, 11 + device scoping sentence | `references/hwg.md` | [verified] |
| HWG § 3a (scope note only) | `references/hwg.md` | [verified] |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 4 | `references/uwg.md` | [verified] |
| UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 | `references/uwg.md` | [verified] |

Swiss market-access requirements are **not** in these files and I have not stated a rule about them — only the UWG consequence if the Swiss claim turns out to be unsupported.

## To close limb (d)

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

It matters more than usual here. Registration is a specific named function, and a quote about changing the registration workflow needs to sit inside the intended purpose the notified body actually assessed for a Class IIb device. A limb (d) problem also can't be fixed with data — it's cured by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The gating does real work, but less than it looks like. Credentialed login to Fachkreise removes the two hardest testimonial hurdles — **§11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 HWG** (advertising that a product is "fachlich empfohlen … oder angewendet") and **§11 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 HWG** (Äußerungen Dritter, Dank-/Empfehlungsschreiben). Both are explicitly limited to advertising *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. A real credential check, not a self-declaration tickbox, is the right design and is defensible.

What gating does **not** touch: **§3 HWG** (Irreführung), **§6 HWG** (Gutachten/Zeugnisse/Zitate), **MDR Art. 7**, and the UWG. Every remaining problem below sits in that untouched set. Both sentences of the copy currently have exposure there.

## Issue 1 — "two steps out of every registration" is an unsubstantiated quantified claim

Quotation marks don't insulate you. German practice is settled that an advertiser who reproduces a third party's statement *macht sie sich zu eigen* — it becomes your performance claim, assessed under §3 HWG and MDR Art. 7(a). Three defects compound:

- **"every registration"** is a universal quantifier attached to one clinician's recollection. It asserts reproducibility across all cases.
- **No baseline.** Two steps fewer than what — your predecessor version, manual registration, a named competitor? If a reader infers a competitor, you're in **§6 UWG** territory (comparison must be objective and verifiable), and an unstated baseline is verifiable by definition never.
- **No source.** This needs a time-and-motion or usability study (IEC 62366 file, PMCF report, CER annex), not a quote.

Germany's Abmahnung culture makes this concrete rather than theoretical — Wettbewerbszentrale and competitors act on exactly this pattern, and the cost order plus Unterlassungserklärung is the real downside.

## Issue 2 — the registration claim has a clinical-safety reading

This is the sharpest point and it's specific to Class IIb navigation. Registration accuracy *is* the safety function. "Fewer steps in registration" can be read by a clinical engineer as "fewer verification steps." Under **MDR Art. 7(c)** (failure to inform of likely risk) and the requirement that promotional material not contradict the IFU, an efficiency claim touching registration should state explicitly that IFU-mandated accuracy-verification steps are unchanged. If the two removed steps *were* verification steps, the claim shouldn't run at all in this form.

## Issue 3 — the named endorser

- **Conflict-of-interest disclosure is mandatory, gated page or not.** If Ellwanger is a paid speaker, advisory board member, received research funding, or the site got discounted/loaner hardware, undisclosed endorsement is getarnte Werbung under **§5a UWG / Anhang zu §3 Abs. 3 Nr. 11**. MedTech Europe's Code of Ethical Business Practice points the same way.
- **Written consent from both the individual and the Klinikum.** Naming the institution implies institutional endorsement; German university hospitals generally require sign-off, and there's Nebentätigkeitsrecht on the clinician's side. Name use in advertising without consent is actionable (§12 BGB, allgemeines Persönlichkeitsrecht).
- **GDPR:** consent is the clean basis, and it's withdrawable — you need an operational path to pull the copy on request.
- **§6 Nr. 3 HWG requires quotes be reproduced *wortgetreu*.** The quote is in English. If he said it in German, the German page must carry his actual words, not a back-translation. Keep the original on file.
- Confirm the title and affiliation are current, and that "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is the institution's exact legal name — an anonymized or composite name that still points at a real site is its own misrepresentation.

## Issue 4 — "in routine use across the DACH region since 2024"

- **Switzerland is the trap.** Since the MRA lapsed in May 2021, CH treats EU devices as third-country: you need an appointed **CH-REP**, Swiss labelling, and MepV registration. Claiming DACH presence asserts you've done this. If there is no Swiss installed base, "DACH" is simply false and should become "Deutschland und Österreich."
- **"Routine use" is a loaded term** — it means standard clinical workflow, not pilot, evaluation, or limited release. If the named site is running an eval unit, the word is wrong there too. Give the site count and the countries.
- **"since 2024" must match the CE certificate and the configuration.** If 2024 experience belongs to a predecessor version or an MDD-era certificate, you cannot transfer that track record to the current device.
- Implicitly this reads as a reliability claim. If there have been FSCAs or vigilance reports on the platform, that reading is a problem.

## Issue 5 — missing mandatory context

No device name, legal manufacturer, Zweckbestimmung, CE mark with Notified Body number, or IFU reference. §4 HWG Pflichtangaben are Arzneimittel-specific and don't bind you here, but MDR requires promotional material be consistent with the IFU, and for a Class IIb device a professional audience should see the intended purpose and an IFU pointer.

**One operational check:** make sure the gated page is `noindex`, excluded from the sitemap, and has no public teaser. If a crawler surfaces the testimonial text, you lose the Fachkreis limitation for that content and §11 HWG comes back into scope.

## Rewrite

**If you can substantiate the claim** (preferred — a cited number is also better marketing):

> In einer Zeit- und Ablaufstudie an [n] Eingriffen am Universitätsklinikum Süd reduzierte sich die Registrierung von [x] auf [y] Arbeitsschritte gegenüber [Vergleichssystem/Vorgängerversion] (Quelle: [Bericht, Datum]). Die in der Gebrauchsanweisung vorgesehenen Schritte zur Genauigkeitsprüfung bleiben unverändert erforderlich.
>
> Prof. Dr. med. [Vorname] Ellwanger, Universitätsklinikum Süd: „[Originalzitat auf Deutsch]"
> Prof. Ellwanger ist [bezahlter Referent / Mitglied des wissenschaftlichen Beirats] von [Hersteller].
>
> [Produktname] ist seit [Monat/Jahr] in Deutschland und Österreich im klinischen Einsatz; Stand [Datum]: [n] Kliniken.
>
> [Produktname], Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIb. CE [NB-Nummer]. Hersteller: [Name, Anschrift]. Zweckbestimmung und vollständige Informationen: Gebrauchsanweisung.

**If you cannot:** drop the quantified sentence entirely and keep the testimonial as a qualitative statement of experience. Do not soften it to "up to two steps" or "in vielen Fällen" — vague quantifiers attract the same challenge without the persuasive benefit.

Separately, I'd put a claims substantiation dossier behind this if one doesn't exist: each claim mapped to its evidence and signed off by regulatory affairs, with the workflow claims traced to the CER or PMCF. It's what makes the difference between answering an Abmahnung in a week and answering it in a quarter.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

The gating does real work here — it likely takes the German testimonial prohibition off the table. But it does nothing for the two claims that carry the most risk: the quantified performance claim and the market-presence claim. Both need substantiation you can produce on demand, and one of them has a clinical-safety framing problem that I'd fix regardless of the legal position.

---

## What the gate buys you

**HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2** bans advertising with recommendations from scientists and health professionals — but only *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. Hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff plausibly fall inside § 2 HWG's Fachkreise definition (institutions serving human health; persons who lawfully trade in or professionally apply medical devices). So a named professorial endorsement is defensible *in this channel*.

Two caveats on that:

- The gate has to actually verify Fachkreis status, not just present a click-through "I am a healthcare professional" interstitial. Credentialed login is the right architecture; confirm registration is vetted rather than self-asserted.
- Gated content leaks — screenshots, sales decks, a credentialed competitor. The realistic German risk vector is an Abmahnung from a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale, and they can get behind a login. Write the copy so it survives being seen outside the gate, even though you're not legally obliged to.

**§ 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung) and MDR Art. 7 apply in full regardless of audience.** These are where your exposure sits.

---

## Findings

### 1. "It took two steps out of every registration" — unsubstantiated quantified claim · High

Three separate problems stacked in one sentence:

- **"Every" is an absolute claim** derived from one clinician's impression at one site. Under § 3 HWG and MDR Art. 7 you need data behind a quantified performance claim, and a quotation mark does not launder an anecdote into evidence. Attributing it to a named user doesn't shift the substantiation burden back to him — you published it.
- **It must match your technical documentation.** If the workflow-step reduction isn't in your clinical evaluation or a validated time-and-motion study, you're claiming performance outside your file. Check it against the registration workflow described in the IFU: if the IFU describes an N-step registration and marketing implies N−2, that discrepancy is the first thing a notified body or opposing counsel will find.
- **The safety framing is wrong for a navigation system.** Registration is the accuracy-critical step in surgical navigation, and some of its steps exist precisely as verification. "We removed two steps from registration" reads to a clinical engineer as *possibly fewer accuracy checks*. Even if what you removed was purely mechanical (fewer fiducial touches, fewer screen confirmations), the copy doesn't say so. State explicitly that verification steps are unchanged. This is the finding I'd act on even if the legal analysis came back clean.

### 2. No disclosure of the relationship with Prof. Ellwanger · High

If he is a consultant, investigator, speaker, or received anything of value, that needs to be disclosed on the page. This is not a formality in Germany:

- **§§ 299a/299b StGB** (Bestechlichkeit/Bestechung im Gesundheitswesen) — an undisclosed paid physician endorsement aimed squarely at procurement decision-makers is the fact pattern those provisions exist for.
- **MedTech Europe Code of Ethical Business Practice** and the German industry codes expect transparency on HCP relationships in promotional material.
- A Universitätsklinikum is a public institution; its employees are typically bound by internal rules on commercial endorsement and secondary-employment disclosure. Confirm he cleared this with his employer, in writing.

If there's no financial relationship at all, say so — "Prof. Ellwanger received no compensation for this statement" is a stronger line than silence.

### 3. "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024" · High

- **Switzerland is not in the EU.** Under the Swiss MepV, market access requires a CH-REP and Swiss-specific labelling. If you're claiming routine Swiss use, confirm that registration was complete for the period claimed. Asserting market presence in CH without it is both a compliance problem and a misleading-advertising problem.
- **"Since 2024" must map to your MDR certificate date.** If early DACH sites were operating under a clinical investigation, a pilot, or limited market release, "routine use" overstates it — routine use means established clinical practice, not evaluation deployments.
- **"Across the region" implies breadth.** Two sites in Bavaria and one in Vienna is not "across DACH." Fix the number of centres and be ready to name the count.

### 4. Consent and institutional name use · Medium

You need documented consent from Prof. Ellwanger for the quote *and* separate permission from the Universitätsklinikum for use of its name. German personality rights and the hospital's trademark/name interests are distinct permissions. Consent should cover this specific wording, this channel, and be revocable-with-notice.

Separately: **"Universitätsklinikum Süd" reads as a placeholder or an anonymisation.** If it's a stand-in, fine. If you've anonymised a real institution into a plausible-sounding fictional one, that's itself misleading — either name it with permission or describe it generically ("a German university hospital").

### 5. Quote fidelity in translation · Medium

If the statement was given in German, the English here is already a translation, and the German page will be a back-translation. "It took two steps out of every registration" is a specific quantified assertion — small translation drift changes what he's on record as saying. Keep the original-language statement as the source of truth and have him approve both versions.

### 6. Device identification · Low

The page should identify the device by name, state that it is a medical device, carry the CE mark with notified body number and manufacturer identity, and direct readers to the IFU. Note that you do **not** need § 4 HWG Pflichtangaben — those apply to Arzneimittel, not Medizinprodukte. Don't over-comply here; it just adds clutter for a procurement audience.

---

## Suggested revision

Conservative version, assuming you can substantiate:

> In a time-and-motion evaluation at [n] centres ([n] registrations), [Device] reduced patient registration from [X] to [Y] operator steps. Accuracy verification steps were unchanged. [Reference to data on file or publication.]
>
> Prof. [Name], [Institution]: "[approved quote]." Prof. [Name] is a paid consultant to [Manufacturer] / received no compensation for this statement.
>
> [Device] has been CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 since [date] and is in clinical use at [n] centres in Germany and Austria. [Swiss availability statement, or omit CH.]

If you want to keep the punch and the claim holds up:

> "It removed two operator steps from every registration — without touching a single verification step." — Prof. [Name], [Institution], paid consultant to [Manufacturer]
>
> Based on [study/data on file]. In clinical use at [n] centres in Germany and Austria since [month/year].

The second keeps the quote's energy while putting the safety qualifier inside the clinician's own words, which is where it lands hardest with a clinical engineering reader.

---

## Verify internally before publishing

1. Is the two-step reduction documented in the clinical evaluation or a study, and does it reconcile with the IFU's registration workflow?
2. Were any of the removed steps verification or accuracy-check steps?
3. What is the financial relationship with Prof. Ellwanger, and is there written consent from him and the institution?
4. Is CH-REP registration complete, and from what date?
5. How many DACH centres, and were any of them under investigation/pilot rather than routine use in 2024?
6. Does the login gate verify Fachkreis status, or does it accept self-assertion?

I've flagged the German-law analysis from the statutory framework as I understand it — HWG § 11 Abs. 1's Fachkreise limitation has been settled since the 2012 amendment, and the Swiss CH-REP requirement since the MepV transition. Given this is Class IIb and the page targets procurement decision-makers, have your regulatory affairs function and German counsel confirm the Fachkreise classification for *your specific* gate design before launch. That classification is load-bearing for the whole testimonial.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

Two sentences, four substantiation gaps, and one probable placeholder. Nothing here is unfixable, but I wouldn't publish it as written even behind a gate — the gate solves a narrower problem than it looks like it solves.

I'm flagging regulatory exposure, not giving legal advice; this needs your PRRC and German counsel to sign off before it goes live.

## "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is almost certainly not a real institution

German university hospitals are named for their city — Heidelberg, Freiburg, Tübingen. There is no "Universitätsklinikum Süd." There's a *Klinikum* Süd in Nürnberg, which is municipal, not university. So this is either a fill-in-the-blank placeholder that escaped into review copy, or a deliberate anonymization. If it's the latter, drop it: a fake-sounding institution attached to a real named professor reads as fabricated to exactly the audience you're targeting, and clinical engineers will try to verify it.

Separately, even with the right name: many German Unikliniken are public bodies with policies against lending their name to commercial endorsement. You need written release from **both** the professor and the Klinikum's press/legal office, not just the professor.

## "It took two steps out of every registration"

This is a quantified performance claim wearing a testimonial costume. Problems, roughly in order of severity:

- **No comparator.** Two steps out of *what* baseline — your previous version, a competitor's system, a manual workflow? If the German navigation market is concentrated enough that procurement will read an unnamed comparator as a specific competitor, you're in implicit comparative advertising under **UWG §6**, which requires the comparison be objective and verifiable on material features.
- **"Every registration" is a universal quantifier.** One surgeon's experience at one site can't support it. Bound it to procedure type, site, and software version.
- **MDR Article 7** prohibits advertising that ascribes functions the device doesn't have or suggests uses outside the certified intended purpose. A workflow-efficiency claim needs to sit inside your intended purpose and trace to something in the technical documentation. Anecdote isn't substantiation.
- **Don't let it drift into clinical benefit.** "Fewer registration steps" is a workflow claim. If the surrounding page lets readers infer shorter anaesthesia time or better accuracy, you've made a clinical claim requiring clinical evidence.
- **Undisclosed relationship.** If Prof. Ellwanger is a consultant, investigator, or has received honoraria, that must be disclosed — **UWG §5a Abs. 4**, plus the BVMed Kodex Medizinprodukte / MedTech Europe transparency expectations. And if he influences purchasing at his own institution while being compensated by you, look hard at **§§299a/b StGB** exposure with counsel.

**The one that usually gets missed:** a specific quantified performance claim made to procurement can be pulled into the supply contract as a warranted characteristic under **§434 BGB** (public statements by the seller inform the agreed condition). "Two steps out of every registration" is exactly the kind of sentence a hospital's legal team quotes back during a warranty dispute. Precision here protects you commercially, not just regulatorily.

## "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024"

- **"Routine use"** (*Routineeinsatz*) implies established standard practice. If this is three reference sites, "across the DACH region" materially overstates adoption. State the number of sites.
- **Switzerland is not the EU.** Claiming Swiss use asserts the device is lawfully on the Swiss market — MepV compliance, a CH-REP, Swissmedic registration. If that isn't in place, cut the "CH" and say Germany and Austria.
- **Check your certificate basis.** For a Class IIb device still riding a legacy MDD certificate under the Regulation 2023/607 transitional extension, make sure nothing on this page implies capability beyond the certified intended purpose.
- **"Since 2024"** needs a verifiable first-install date on file.

## What the gate actually buys you

A genuine credential-verified gate to *Fachkreise* likely disapplies **HWG §11 Abs. 1** — the restrictions on expert recommendations and third-party statements that apply outside professional circles. Hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff have a reasonable claim to Fachkreise status under **HWG §2**, though it's worth an explicit legal opinion rather than an assumption.

What the gate does **not** disapply, at all:

- **HWG §3** — the prohibition on misleading advertising applies to Fachkreise advertising too
- **MDR Article 7** — audience-independent
- **UWG §5, §5a, §6**
- Transparency obligations on HCP relationships

And practically: this copy will not stay behind the gate. Sales will paste it into a deck, marketing into a LinkedIn post, someone into a tender response. The moment it does, the §11 analysis collapses. Write it so it survives outside the gate.

## Suggested rewrite

> Prof. Dr. [Full Name], [Department], Universitätsklinikum [City]:
> "In our [procedure type] workflow, [Product] removed two steps from each patient registration compared with [named prior workflow/system]."
>
> *Translated from German; original statement on file. Prof. [Name] is a paid consultant to [Manufacturer] / received no compensation for this statement.* Single-centre user experience with [Product] software v[X.Y]. Individual results may vary; this does not represent evidence of clinical benefit.
>
> [Product] has been in clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [Month] 2024.

Two things in there worth keeping deliberately: the translation note (a German quote rendered in English can shift meaning — was it *Schritte* or *Arbeitsschritte*?), and the named comparator, which is what converts an unverifiable boast into a defensible statement.

## Before publish

1. Confirm the institution name and hold written release from the professor **and** the Klinikum.
2. Log both claims in your claims matrix with evidence references and PRRC sign-off (MDR Art. 15).
3. Confirm Swiss market status or cut Switzerland.
4. Verify the gate does real credential checking, not a self-declaration checkbox — German courts have treated click-through declarations as insufficient.
5. Version-control the page and archive it with dates; procurement will cite what they saw.
6. Make sure the page carries device name, intended purpose, manufacturer, CE mark with Notified Body number, and an IFU reference — your audience expects it, and it constrains how the testimonial reads.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: consumer web page, home BP monitor

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (ungated public consumer page) → HWG § 11(1) applies, nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only
**Markets:** EU + DE

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.**

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The fear-framing sentence is the problem, and it's the highest-frequency HWG breach in consumer device copy. The endorsement is *not* automatically prohibited — the rule people usually reach for here (§ 11(1) no. 2, professional endorsements) does not apply to medical devices at all.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Publikumswerbung "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte". The gamble metaphor states exactly that: not measuring puts your heart at risk. Paired with "check your pressure daily", it also creates an outcome impression — that measuring protects the heart — from a device that measures and does not treat. That is Art. 7(b), "creating a false impression regarding treatment".
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. The defect is the framing, not a missing substantiation.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "gamble" frames non-use as chance and use as certainty, which edges toward "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". Secondary to the no. 7 point, but it survives if you soften the fear wording without removing the certainty implication.
**Call:** **Cut**

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A measurement-frequency instruction is not misleading in itself. But a daily regimen stated in advertising is a usage direction, and whether it matches the IFU and the assessed intended purpose is unverifiable without those documents. It also carries the § 11(1) no. 7 sentence it is attached to — severed from "don't gamble", it reads very differently.
**Evidence needed:** the IFU's measurement guidance, and the intended purpose as assessed.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") `[verified]` — if the IFU specifies a different regimen, or defers frequency to the treating physician.
**Call:** **Needs rewording** (and verify against the IFU)

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 11 covers "Äußerungen Dritter, insbesondere [...] Empfehlungsschreiben" — but only "wenn diese in **missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender** Weise erfolgen". Testimonials are not prohibited for devices. Nothing in the quote is misleading on its face. Note explicitly: **§ 11(1) no. 2 — the professional-endorsement prohibition — does not apply**, because the closing sentence of § 11(1) limits devices to nos. 7 to 9, 11 and 12. Citing no. 2 here would be a false positive.
**Evidence needed:** Schmidt's full name, title, specialty registration and institution; written confirmation of the recommendation and its current validity; disclosure of any commercial relationship (fee, advisory board, equity, research funding).
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — "Angaben über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge [...] der für sie tätigen [...] Personen" — bites if Schmidt is engaged by the manufacturer and the title or specialty is overstated.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]` — "Befähigung, Status" — bites if "Professor" or "cardiologist" is not accurate.
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — bites as *irreführend* if a paid relationship is undisclosed, or the recommendation is stale or never given in those terms.

**Practical note:** "Professor Schmidt" with no first name and no institution cannot be checked by any reader. Per the UWG reference, a broad and unverifiable claim is expensive to defend even when it is true. Naming him fully costs nothing and removes most of the exposure.
**Call:** **Verify**

---

## Paste-ready replacement

**EN:**
> Recommended by Prof. Dr. med. [full name], Cardiologist, [institution]. [Paid advisor to / No commercial relationship with] [company].
> Measure your blood pressure at home. Discuss your readings with your doctor. Follow the measurement schedule in the instructions for use.

**DE:**
> Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. med. [vollständiger Name], Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Einrichtung]. [Bezahlter Berater von / Keine geschäftliche Beziehung zu] [Unternehmen].
> Messen Sie Ihren Blutdruck zu Hause. Besprechen Sie Ihre Werte mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt. Beachten Sie die Angaben in der Gebrauchsanweisung.

What changed and why: the gamble/fear framing is gone entirely — note that § 11(1) no. 7 bans *both* directions, so "improve your heart health by measuring daily" is not a safe substitute either. The copy now describes function rather than promising an outcome, the frequency defers to the IFU, and the "discuss with your doctor" line is the proportionate way to signal that readings need clinical interpretation.

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU — but I am not raising (c) as a finding, because I would be inferring the risk from the device category rather than from your documents, and a finding built that way is unfalsifiable.

## Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

It matters specifically for "check your pressure daily" and for the cardiology endorsement, which frames the device in a cardiac-risk context. Note the cure path differs: an (a) overclaim can be fixed with evidence; a (d) breach cannot — it is fixed by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Prof. Schmidt endorsement | Full name, title, specialty registration, institution | Marketing / the endorser |
| Prof. Schmidt endorsement | Signed, dated, currently valid recommendation | Legal / the endorser |
| Prof. Schmidt endorsement | Commercial relationship disclosure | Legal / finance |
| "check your pressure daily" | IFU measurement guidance | Regulatory / technical file |
| All claims | Intended purpose as assessed (DoC / tech doc) | Regulatory |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), Art. 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), § 3 no. 3(b), § 11(1) no. 7, § 11(1) no. 11 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 5(2) no. 3 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

No case law cited. Whether this particular fear-framing has been litigated, and how German courts treat undisclosed physician endorsements, turns on sources this skill does not verify — I won't state a rule I can't cite from the reference files.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum — ungated public consumer page. HWG § 11 applies (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only)
**Markets:** DE (EU层 MDR Art. 7 also applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

The fear clause is the problem, and it is not fixable by evidence. The endorsement is not prohibited — that is the most common false positive in this area — but it carries conditions you need to check.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Publikumswerbung "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte". "Don't gamble with your heart" says exactly that: not measuring puts your heart at risk. It is the textbook shape of no. 7. Art. 7(b) is engaged in parallel — pairing cardiac jeopardy with a measurement instruction creates a false impression that the act of measuring confers cardiac protection, which is an outcome a monitoring device does not deliver.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Even a device that measures perfectly cannot carry this framing to a lay audience.
**Call:** Cut

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A measurement-frequency instruction is not misleading in itself. But it is a usage recommendation, and its lawfulness depends on whether daily self-measurement sits inside the intended purpose the conformity assessment covered and matches the IFU's measurement regimen. Standing next to the cut clause, it also picks up the "Verwendung verbessert" half of § 11(1) no. 7; standing alone after the rewrite, it does not.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — if the assessed intended purpose or the IFU does not support a daily self-measurement regimen, or frames measurement as physician-directed. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") on the same condition.
**Call:** Verify, then reword as below

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Note first what does **not** apply: HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (endorsements by scientists and healthcare professionals) is **disapplied for medical devices** by the closing sentence of § 11(1) — "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend." A cardiologist endorsement on a device page is not prohibited as such. The applicable item is no. 11, which reaches third-party Äußerungen only "wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen". Nothing in the quoted words is misleading on its face. What makes it fragile is that a bare surname with no institution, no date, and no stated relationship is not checkable by the reader.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — if the recommendation is not genuine, not current, or if a commercial relationship (fee, equity, consultancy) is undisclosed
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — "über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung" of persons working for the manufacturer: if "Professor" or "cardiologist" overstates the actual title or specialty
- HWG § 11(1) no. 9 `[verified]` — if the endorsement is paid and the surrounding page does not make the promotional purpose clearly recognisable
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]` — same facts, as the enforcement route

**Call:** Verify

### Suggested fix — paste-ready

The asset is under 50 words, so here is the actual revised copy rather than a description.

> Recommended by Prof. Dr. med. [full name], Cardiologist, [institution]. Regular blood-pressure measurement at home helps you and your doctor track your readings over time. Follow the measurement schedule in the instructions for use and discuss your results with your doctor.

German rendering, since the page runs in DE:

> Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. med. [voller Name], Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Klinik/Institution]. Die regelmäßige Blutdruckmessung zu Hause hilft Ihnen und Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt, Ihre Werte über die Zeit zu verfolgen. Beachten Sie das Messintervall in der Gebrauchsanweisung und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte ärztlich.

What the rewrite does: drops the jeopardy framing entirely (no. 7), replaces the protective implication with a factual statement of what the device does (Art. 7(b)), makes the endorser identifiable so no. 11 and § 3 no. 3(b) have something to be true against, and defers the measurement frequency to the IFU rather than asserting "daily" from the ad. If Prof. Schmidt is compensated, add a disclosure line adjacent to the endorsement — not in a footer.

Keep "daily" only if the IFU specifies it.

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I cannot tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for a Class IIa monitor the candidates are things like measurement conditions, cuff fit, or arrhythmia affecting validity, but I am not going to flag an omission against a risk I am inferring from the device category rather than reading in your material. Check the copy against the IFU's warnings section; if a likely risk is recorded there, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix for a short web asset.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Full name, verified title, Facharzt designation, institution | Regulatory / marketing |
| Same | Written, current endorsement on file; date | Marketing |
| Same | Whether any fee, equity or consultancy exists — drives disclosure | Legal / commercial |
| "daily" | Measurement regimen as stated in the IFU | Regulatory |

# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum — ungated public consumer page. HWG § 11 applies (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only)
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 clean as written.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The headline problem is the fear framing, not the endorsement. Note that the endorsement is **not** caught by HWG § 11(1) no. 2 — that item does not extend to medical devices (§ 11(1) closing sentence: *"Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend"*). Only no. 11 reaches it, and no. 11 has a qualifier.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits copy *"die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die Nichtverwendung [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte"*. "Gamble with your heart" says exactly that: not measuring puts your heart at risk. Art. 7(b) bites in parallel — a monitoring device measures; it does not reduce cardiac risk, so the copy creates a false impression regarding treatment from a measurement-only device.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is framing, not a factual claim, and no study makes a fear appeal lawful under no. 7.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** Replace the risk-of-not-using frame with a use frame: "Regular measurement gives you and your doctor a clearer picture of your blood pressure over time."

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — as written, in this sentence
**Why:** No. 7 also catches the positive half — health *"durch die Verwendung verbessert werden könnte"*. Standing alone, a frequency instruction is neutral; joined to "don't gamble with your heart" by the dash, it reads as "measure daily and your heart is safer". Cutting the first half largely defuses this one.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — **if** the assessed intended purpose or the IFU specifies a measurement regimen (e.g. measurement on medical advice, or a defined morning/evening protocol) rather than unilateral daily self-measurement. A directive daily frequency that the technical documentation does not support is intended-purpose drift, and it is cured by narrowing the claim, not by data. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — *"von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"* — is engaged on the same facts.
**Evidence needed:** The intended purpose as assessed, and the IFU's stated measurement frequency.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "Follow the measurement schedule your doctor recommends, and discuss your readings with them."

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 11 covers *Äußerungen Dritter* — third-party recommendations — but only *"wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen"*. Testimonials are not flatly prohibited for devices, and the professional-endorsement item (§ 11(1) no. 2) does not apply to devices at all. Nothing in the quoted words is misleading on its face.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — if the person is not identifiable, not a cardiologist, holds no professorship, or did not give the recommendation in these terms, it becomes *irreführend* and the item bites.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — *"über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge [...] der für sie tätigen [...] Personen"* — if Schmidt is engaged by or works for the manufacturer, the accuracy of "Professor" and "cardiologist" is tested here directly.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]` — *"Beziehungen"* — if there is a paid or equity relationship presented as an independent recommendation.
- No. 11 again, contextually: the endorsement currently sits beside the fear appeal and lends it clinical authority. Fixing the second sentence removes that interaction.
**Evidence needed:** Schmidt's full name and title, verification of the professorship and the Facharzt qualification, the signed recommendation or its written basis, and the nature of any commercial relationship.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix (if the relationship is commercial):** "Recommended by Prof. Dr. [full name], cardiologist — paid advisor to [company]."

---

### Paste-ready revision

> Recommended by Prof. Dr. [full name], cardiologist [add disclosure if the relationship is commercial]. Regular measurement gives you and your doctor a clearer picture of your blood pressure over time. Follow the measurement schedule your doctor recommends, and discuss your readings with them.

The page will publish in German; have the copywriter check that the German rendering does not reintroduce a *Nichtverwendung* implication, which is easy to do with phrasings like "nicht dem Zufall überlassen".

## Open question on limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for a home BP monitor, candidates would be cuff-size or arrhythmia limitations affecting reading validity, or an instruction not to change medication based on self-measured readings. I am not raising (c) on inference. Check the IFU: if it records such a risk, the proportionate fix on a consumer page is usually a short pointer to the instructions for use rather than full safety text.

## Verdict

Both halves of this line have problems. I'd not ship it as written.

The key structural fact: **no gating means this is *Laienwerbung*** (advertising outside professional circles), so the full restrictive regime of the **Heilmittelwerbegesetz (HWG)** applies, alongside **MDR Art. 7** and the **UWG**. Class IIa is squarely in scope — the HWG covers medical devices, and §11 Abs. 1's chapeau reaches "Gegenstände oder andere Mittel," not just medicinal products.

---

## 1. "Don't gamble with your heart" — highest risk

This is textbook *Angstwerbung*. **HWG §11 Abs. 1** prohibits lay-directed advertising with statements "geeignet, Angstgefühle hervorzurufen oder auszunutzen" — apt to create or exploit anxiety. The gambling metaphor does exactly that: it frames non-purchase as reckless endangerment of your own heart.

Unlike some neighbouring provisions (which the 2012 amendment narrowed to *Arzneimittel*), the fear-appeal prohibition is drafted against the general chapeau and reaches devices. **Confirm the current numbering and scope with German regulatory counsel** — the post-2012 HWG has drug-limited and general items interleaved, and which is which matters here.

**Cut it.** There is no safe-harbour version of "don't gamble with your heart."

## 2. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — high risk

Three separate exposures:

**HWG.** The prohibition on advertising with professional recommendation/endorsement (§11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2) is, in its current wording, drafted around *Arzneimittel* — so a literal reading may not catch a device. Do not rely on that gap. German courts apply a heightened truthfulness standard (*Strengeprinzip*) to health advertising, and an HCP endorsement aimed at consumers is precisely the authority-transfer the regime exists to prevent.

**UWG §5 / §5a Abs. 4.** If Prof. Schmidt was paid, holds equity, or has any commercial relationship with you, non-disclosure is *Schleichwerbung*. If the endorsement is embellished, stale, or — worst case — a composite or invented figure, you are in the UWG blacklist territory of falsely claiming approval.

**Substantiation.** "Professor Schmidt" with no institution, no first name, and one of the most common surnames in Germany is functionally unverifiable. That weakness cuts against you, not for you: an unverifiable authority claim reads as puffery at best and misleading at worst.

**Before this line could survive at all** you'd need: a documented, current, written endorsement; full identification (name, title, institution); disclosure of any financial relationship; and counsel sign-off on the HWG point. Even then I'd advise against it — see the replacement below, which is both safer *and* more persuasive.

## 3. "Check your pressure daily" — moderate risk

This is a clinical instruction issued to an ungated general audience, and it doesn't match guidance. ESH/ESC and the Deutsche Hochdruckliga recommend structured home monitoring — typically 7-day schedules, morning and evening, duplicate readings — for people with known or suspected hypertension, not blanket daily measurement for everyone.

Two consequences: it's misleading under **MDR Art. 7** and **UWG §5**, and it likely **contradicts your own IFU**. Promotional material must be consistent with the intended purpose and instructions for use; divergence is a technical-documentation and QMS finding, not just a marketing one. Check this line against the IFU before anything else.

---

## Suggested rewrite

Replace the borrowed authority with real, verifiable substantiation. For a BP monitor the strong trust signal is validation status, which you can state plainly and defend:

> **EN:** "Clinically validated to ISO 81060-2. Know your numbers — measure at home and share your readings with your doctor."
>
> **DE:** "Klinisch validiert nach ISO 81060-2. Kennen Sie Ihre Werte — messen Sie zu Hause und besprechen Sie Ihre Ergebnisse mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt."

Only claim ISO 81060-2 if you actually hold it. If you're listed on STRIDE BP or carry the **Deutsche Hochdruckliga Prüfsiegel**, lead with that instead — for a German consumer it outperforms any individual cardiologist's name.

For frequency, defer rather than instruct: "Measure as often as your doctor recommends." Add a short "not a substitute for medical advice" line and clear "Medizinprodukt" signposting — good practice for consumer device pages, though the specific mandatory-disclosure rules here are worth confirming with counsel.

---

## Two things I need from you

1. **Is Prof. Schmidt a real, identifiable person who has given a documented endorsement?** If it's a composite or illustrative placeholder, that's a straightforward false-advertising problem and the line has to go regardless of the HWG analysis.
2. **What does the IFU say about measurement frequency?** I flagged the mismatch from guidelines, but I can't verify the IFU conflict without seeing it.

One process note: this copy will publish in German. Have the translation reviewed on its own, not just signed off as equivalent — fear framing and authority claims shift in force across languages, and the German text is what regulators and competitors will read.

I've given you the substantive analysis, but treat the specific HWG subsection numbering as requiring confirmation by qualified German regulatory counsel before you rely on it.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't publish as written. Both sentences carry a distinct legal problem under German law, and the combination is close to a textbook Abmahnung target.

---

## Blocker 1 — "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist"

**Problem:** Publikumswerbung (advertising to the general public) for a medical device may not claim that the product is professionally recommended, tested, or used by a doctor. This is § 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 2 HWG. The HWG applies to medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG, referencing Art. 2 Nr. 1 MDR), so Class IIa is squarely in scope.

The decisive fact here is **"no gating."** This restriction only applies *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. If the page were behind a verified HCP gate, the claim would be assessable on ordinary substantiation grounds instead. Ungated, it's a per-se violation regardless of whether Prof. Schmidt genuinely holds that view.

Secondary exposure on the same line:
- **The doctor's own risk.** § 27 of the Musterberufsordnung für Ärzte prohibits physicians from lending their name/professional standing to product advertising. You may be inducing a professional-conduct breach by a named third party.
- **Testimonial transparency.** If the recommendation is compensated in any form (fee, honorarium, equipment, advisory board), UWG § 5a Abs. 4 requires the commercial nature to be disclosed. Undisclosed = separate violation.
- **Substantiation.** "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" is unverifiable as written — no institution, no basis. Even setting HWG aside, that's weak under § 3 HWG / § 5 UWG.

**Fix:** Remove it. Don't try to rescue it with softer phrasing ("trusted by cardiologists," "developed with cardiologists") — the prohibition covers the substance, not the wording. Replace the credibility function with something legally durable: clinical validation of measurement accuracy (e.g. tested to ISO 81060-2, if true), Notified Body CE marking, or independent test results such as Stiftung Warentest ratings, which are permissible if accurately and non-misleadingly cited.

---

## Blocker 2 — "Don't gamble with your heart"

**Problem:** This is Angstwerbung — it implies that health may be harmed by *not* using the product. Prohibited in public-facing advertising under § 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 7 HWG. "Gamble with your heart" is an unusually explicit instance: it frames non-purchase as a cardiac risk.

It also engages **MDR Art. 7**, which independently bans claims that create a false impression regarding diagnosis or that exploit the user's vulnerability.

**Fix:** Reframe from threat to benefit/empowerment. "Keep an eye on your blood pressure" is fine. "Or else" is not.

---

## Issue 3 — "check your pressure daily"

This is a usage instruction, and it must match your **intended purpose as assessed by the Notified Body** (MDR Art. 7(d) forbids suggesting uses other than those covered by the conformity assessment). Two things to check:

1. Does your IFU actually instruct daily measurement? If it specifies a structured schedule (the Deutsche Hochdruckliga / ESH pattern is typically 7 consecutive days, morning and evening, around diagnosis or treatment adjustment), the ad contradicts your own documentation.
2. Blanket daily self-measurement isn't clinically indicated for normotensive users and is associated with measurement anxiety. Advising it universally to an ungated consumer audience is hard to defend.

**Fix:** Either align exactly with the IFU wording, or use a neutral formulation that doesn't prescribe a frequency.

---

## Also missing from the page

- Identification as a medical device and the **intended purpose** in plain language.
- A pointer to the Gebrauchsanweisung / a hinweis to read it.
- Manufacturer identity and CE mark with Notified Body number (required on the device/labelling; good practice on the product page).

---

## Suggested rewrite

**EN:** "Clinically validated home blood pressure monitor, tested for measurement accuracy to ISO 81060-2. Regular readings help you and your doctor keep track of your blood pressure. Medical device — please read the instructions for use."

**DE:** „Klinisch validiertes Blutdruckmessgerät für zu Hause – Messgenauigkeit geprüft nach ISO 81060-2. Regelmäßige Messungen helfen Ihnen und Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt, Ihren Blutdruck im Blick zu behalten. Medizinprodukt – bitte Gebrauchsanweisung beachten."

Only keep the ISO 81060-2 line if you hold the validation data; otherwise substitute what you can evidence.

---

**Two caveats.** I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice — have your regulatory counsel confirm the exact HWG subsection numbering before you rely on it in a review record, since § 11 Abs. 1 was restructured in 2012 and several items were narrowed. And note the enforcement reality: in Germany, HWG breaches are actionable by competitors and by bodies like the Wettbewerbszentrale and Verbraucherzentralen via Abmahnung, and are also an Ordnungswidrigkeit under § 15 HWG. Enforcement doesn't wait for a regulator to notice.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: don't publish. Both sentences are independently problematic under German law.

This is a regulatory read, not legal advice — get your German counsel or regulatory affairs to sign off before launch.

---

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — Stop

**HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 2** prohibits advertising to the general public (*außerhalb der Fachkreise*) with statements that a product is medically or otherwise professionally recommended, tested, or used. The HWG applies to medical devices via § 1 Abs. 1, so a Class IIa BP monitor is squarely in scope.

This is close to the textbook example of a violation. It doesn't matter whether:

- Professor Schmidt is real and genuinely recommends it,
- the recommendation is unpaid,
- you disclose the relationship.

The prohibition attaches to the *format* — a named healthcare professional endorsing the product to consumers — not to its truthfulness. Disclosure fixes the separate § 5a UWG covert-advertising problem; it does not fix this one.

A second hook is **§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 11** (third-party statements, testimonials, letters of recommendation, or references to them). Note that § 11 Abs. 1 Satz 2 carves certain numbered items out for medical devices — have counsel confirm which apply; Nr. 2 is the one I'd rely on regardless.

**Exposure:** HWG is a *Marktverhaltensregelung* under § 3a UWG, so this is actionable by competitors, the Wettbewerbszentrale, and Verbraucherzentralen via § 8 UWG — typically an *Abmahnung* demanding a *Unterlassungserklärung* with a contractual penalty. Cheap to file, expensive to receive.

**Fix:** remove entirely. There is no gated-audience workaround on a public consumer page — the whole point of the rule is the lay audience. If you want the endorsement, it can live in HCP-facing materials behind genuine professional-verification gating, which is a different asset with a different approval path.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — Stop

**HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 7** prohibits advertising statements likely to cause or exploit feelings of fear (*Angstwerbung*). Framing non-use as gambling with your heart is a fear appeal in the most direct sense: it implies that not buying the product exposes you to cardiac risk.

### 3. "check your pressure daily" — Fix

Two separate issues:

- **Off-label usage instruction.** If your IFU and intended purpose don't specify daily measurement, the copy is promoting a use pattern outside the approved intended purpose — **MDR Art. 7(d)**. Check what your IFU actually says. German and European hypertension guidance generally frames home monitoring as structured measurement series (e.g. morning/evening over ~7 days around a clinical review), not indefinite daily use, so "daily" may also be clinically unsupported.
- **Implied clinical benefit.** Read with sentence 2, the combined message is "daily measurement protects you from cardiac events." A BP monitor measures; it does not prevent. That's a false impression regarding the device's properties under **MDR Art. 7(b)** and misleading under **MPDG § 14**.

### 4. Language — Watch

For the German market, run the final copy in German. Device labelling and IFU must be in German (MDR Art. 10(11) / MPDG); advertising in English isn't per se unlawful but invites an "unclear to the average German consumer" argument, and you need the German wording legally reviewed anyway since that's what you'll publish.

---

## Suggested replacement

**German:**

> **[Produktname] – Blutdruck messen zu Hause.**
> Misst systolischen und diastolischen Blutdruck sowie den Puls am Oberarm und speichert bis zu [n] Messwerte.
> Erfüllt die Anforderungen der ISO 81060-2.
> Besprechen Sie Ihre Messwerte und die für Sie passende Messhäufigkeit mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.

**English gloss:** measures systolic/diastolic BP and pulse at the upper arm, stores up to [n] readings, meets ISO 81060-2, discuss your readings and the right measurement frequency with your doctor.

Why this works: factual function description tied to the intended purpose, no named endorser, no fear frame, and it routes the clinical judgement (how often to measure) to the treating physician rather than making it a marketing claim.

One drafting note on the validation line: **avoid "klinisch geprüft" or "ärztlich geprüft."** *Geprüft* is a trigger word in § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 alongside *empfohlen*. Stating conformity with a named standard ("erfüllt die Anforderungen der ISO 81060-2") is a factual product statement rather than a professional endorsement, which is the safer framing — but it's a grey zone worth putting in front of counsel.

---

## What I'd need to confirm the rewrite

1. Your **intended purpose and IFU wording** — specifically whether measurement frequency is specified, and whether the device is indicated for a particular population (adults only? pregnancy? atrial fibrillation?).
2. Which **validation standard and protocol** you actually hold evidence for, so the conformity line is substantiated.
3. Whether you have any **arrhythmia detection or irregular-heartbeat indicator** feature — if so it needs its own carefully bounded claim, as it's the most common source of over-claiming on these devices.

# Device Claims Review: CGM launch copy (3 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Ambiguous — **assumed Publikum** (patient-facing: "your phone", "at a glance"). Confirm; if this is trade-press or HCP-gated, § 11 drops out and § 3 still applies.
**Markets:** Assumed EU. **DE not confirmed** — HWG/UWG items below are marked as contingent on the German market.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 to verify, 0 OK as written.**

The intended purpose you supplied carries an express limitation — readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change. The copy's closing line points at exactly the use that limitation excludes, and nothing in the copy surfaces the limitation. That is the whole finding set; the first two lines are fixable wording, the third is not.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed (paste-ready copy at the end).

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`, and MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out." Insulin dosing is a treatment decision, and your assessed intended purpose expressly carves out treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. Unqualified "dose with confidence" suggests the readings are a sufficient basis for dosing in all conditions, including the excluded one. Art. 7(b) is engaged in parallel: it prohibits "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis", and the line creates precisely a treatment impression — the word "confidence" does the work of telling the reader no confirmation is needed.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — **cannot be cured by evidence.** This is the cure-path distinction that matters here: no accuracy dataset fixes a (d) finding. It is cured by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to a non-adjunctive dosing indication. If the device *is* assessed for non-adjunctive dosing, then the intended purpose you pasted is not the one that governs and I should review against the right one.
**Also engaged:** If the copy targets Germany — HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]` (effects the device does not have, tracking the Art. 7(b) point), and arguably § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]`, "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". I flag no. 2(a) as arguable rather than clear: "with confidence" is an assurance of reliability, not literally a guarantee of outcome, and whether it reads as *Sicherheit* is a question of how the provision is applied in practice — which is case law this review does not assess.
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** "Confirm with a blood glucose test before dosing when your glucose is changing rapidly."

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** (c) is an omission test — copy containing nothing false still breaches it by "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose." The risk here is not inferred from the device category; it is **named in the intended purpose you supplied**: readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change. A patient acting on a rapid-change reading as if it were a blood glucose value is a risk arising from use in line with the intended purpose, and this copy surfaces none of it. "At a glance" compounds it by framing the reading as needing no interpretation or confirmation.

Secondary, weaker point: the device measures **interstitial** glucose; "your glucose" reads as blood glucose. On its own I would treat that as a drafting note rather than an Art. 7(a) finding — but it is the same gap the (c) finding is about, and one word fixes both.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by adding the limitation, not by data. Proportionality note: three lines of launch copy are not expected to carry full IFU safety text. A single qualifying sentence, or an IFU pointer, is the proportionate fix.
**Also engaged:** DE — HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` was considered and I do **not** think it bites: the copy does not suggest health is impaired by non-use or improved by use. Noting it so you can see it was checked, not raised.
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Know your glucose trends at a glance."

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A specific, narrow, verifiable performance claim of the kind that is cheap to defend. The 5-minute interval and the phone delivery are factual and checkable against the technical file. Two soft spots, neither a breach on the material in front of me: "real-time" sits awkwardly with the interstitial-to-blood lag that is the mechanism behind your own rapid-change carve-out, and "readings" unqualified reads as blood glucose.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the 5-minute interval is the specified measurement/display interval in the technical documentation (not a typical or best-case figure), and check whether the IFU characterises output as real-time.
**Also engaged:** DE — UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("wesentliche Merkmale [...] von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"), if the 5-minute figure is nominal rather than specified.
**Call:** **Verify** — and reword "real-time" to "continuous" if the IFU does not use real-time language.
**Suggested fix:** "Continuous interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."

---

## Paste-ready revised copy

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.** Continuous interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing rapidly, confirm with a blood glucose test before dosing.

This keeps the three-beat rhythm and the "straight to your phone" hook. The third line changes job — from a dosing promise to a dosing instruction — which is what removes the (d) exposure and closes the (c) omission at the same time.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Dose with confidence" | The intended purpose **as assessed** — confirm whether any non-adjunctive dosing indication is within the conformity assessment scope. If yes, this review is against the wrong anchor. | RA / technical documentation owner |
| "every 5 minutes" | Specified measurement and display interval, as stated in the technical file | R&D / RA |
| "Real-time" | Whether the IFU characterises output as real-time; the stated interstitial-to-blood lag | RA / clinical |
| Whole asset | Confirm target market (DE or not) and audience (Publikum or Fachkreise) | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a)** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` — contingent on German market
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` — considered, not raised
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` — contingent

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things would sharpen this if you can supply them: the **market** (the German overlay is currently all conditional) and confirmation that the intended purpose you pasted is the one the conformity assessment actually covered. If the device holds a non-adjunctive dosing indication, the "Dose with confidence" finding changes from Cut to a wording question.
