**Markets:** DE (+ EU)

## Summary

1 claim reviewed. 1 needs rewording + substantiation.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Finding

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."
**Breach:** HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 3 no. 1 prohibits attributing to a Gegenstand a "therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen, die sie nicht haben". Art. 7(a) is the same test at EU level. The copy asserts a specific quantified therapeutic effect. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 reaches it twice over — as "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and as the "Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**", since a bare "40%" presents a study result stripped of its essential components (comparator, endpoint, n, significance).
**The independent defect, separate from evidence:** the claim has **no comparator**. 40% faster *than what* — untreated, standard gauze, a named competitor, your own previous generation? An unanchored percentage is not capable of being true or false, which makes it misleading on its face regardless of what the study shows.
**Evidence needed:** Data establishing the 40% figure against a stated comparator on a defined healing endpoint. Whether n=12, in-house and unpublished supports a quantified public efficacy claim is **exactly the case-law question above** — the statute tells you the claim must not attribute effects the device does not have; it does not tell you the evidentiary threshold for showing that it does. That threshold is the part I can't source.
**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** — "Heals" in the flat indicative, unhedged, presents the outcome as assured rather than observed. Would not bite on "showed a 40% reduction in...".
- **UWG § 6(2) nos. 1 and 2** — *if* the surrounding asset makes a Mitbewerber erkennbar (§ 6(1) is broad; naming isn't required). Then the comparison must be "nachprüfbar" — and an unpublished in-house study is not checkable by the reader from public information, which is the limb that fails most often.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** — only if the audience is Publikum. I'm flagging this as an **open question, not a breach**: no. 7 catches health-improvement-by-use framing, but a wound dressing's assessed purpose *is* wound healing, and whether a core therapeutic claim falls inside no. 7 is case-law-shaped. Don't let me call it.

**Call:** Needs rewording **and** substantiation — and the rewording is required even if the data holds up.

**Suggested fix** (paste-ready; fill the bracket, and only use it if the data actually says this):

> DE: „In einer internen Anwendungsbeobachtung (n = 12, nicht publiziert) verkürzte sich die mittlere Zeit bis zum Wundverschluss gegenüber [Vergleichsprodukt / Standardversorgung] um 40 %."
>
> EN: "In an internal clinical observation (n = 12, unpublished), mean time to wound closure was 40% shorter compared with [comparator]."

That version names the comparator, names the endpoint, and discloses n and publication status on the face of the claim — which is what takes it out of § 5(2) no. 1's "Tests" hook. It does **not** resolve whether n=12 is enough to make the claim at all.

## Two things I need to finish this

| Gap | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Intended purpose as assessed**, verbatim from the DoC/technical documentation | Limb (d) is unassessed. If the assessed purpose is, say, exudate management or moist wound environment rather than accelerated healing, "heals 40% faster" is an intended-purpose breach that **evidence cannot cure** — it's fixed by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment. For a wound dressing this is a live risk, not a formality. |
| **Audience** — gated Fachkreise, or public page? | Decides whether § 11 applies at all. A B2B page anyone can load is not automatically Fachkreise. |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1–2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Three questions to take to counsel**, since the substantiation standard is the one I can't source:

1. What evidentiary standard applies to a quantified efficacy claim for a Class IIa device in German-market advertising, and does an unpublished in-house study at n=12 meet it?
2. Who carries the burden if we're abmahnt — do we have to produce the substantiation, or does the challenger have to disprove the claim?
3. Does disclosing n and the unpublished status on the face of the claim change the analysis, or is a claim that can't be publicly verified exposed under § 6(2) no. 2 regardless?

graders.evidence:
Web search was denied in this session, so I couldn't verify the citations. Below I've marked what's settled doctrine versus what you must have counsel confirm before relying on it. Treat every case number as unverified.

## The framing needs a correction first

There isn't a BGH decision I'm aware of that is *the* medical-device efficacy case. The BGH doesn't run a device-specific substantiation standard. It applies one general standard to **gesundheitsbezogene Werbung** (health-related advertising) across pharmaceuticals, devices, foods and treatments, developed mostly in pharma cases and then imported. So "the leading case" is a pharma case, and that is not a weakness in the answer — it is how the doctrine is structured.

## The standard (high confidence — settled, repeatedly restated)

**The Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is subject to "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit" of the claim, because the protected interest is health, not just wallet.

**The substantive test:** an efficacy claim must correspond to **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** — secured scientific knowledge — at the time the claim is made.

**The burden of proof is reversed.** Normally a plaintiff proves a statement misleading. Here, once a claimant alleges the claim lacks scientific backing, the *advertiser* carries the burden of proving it. You cannot assemble the evidence after the Abmahnung lands; the substantiation must have existed when the copy ran.

**The evidentiary gold standard:** a randomised, placebo/comparator-controlled, double-blind study with adequate patient numbers and proper statistical evaluation, conducted per recognised scientific rules. Lower-grade evidence isn't automatically fatal, but it does not sustain a hard quantified efficacy claim.

**Publication matters.** The BGH line holds that results must be accessible to scientific discussion. An unpublished in-house study is weak precisely because it has never been exposed to that scrutiny. *(Medium confidence on this being stated in the leading case specifically — verify.)*

## The case citation (verify before use)

**BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). My recollection is this is the standard modern citation for the gold-standard requirement and the burden allocation. I'm reasonably but not fully confident in the date and docket number, and I will not give you a German-language verbatim quote from memory — that is exactly the thing that gets fabricated. Have counsel pull the Leitsätze.

## Applying it to your facts

Your copy fails on several independent grounds, and this does not turn on which case you cite:

1. **n=12 cannot support "40% faster."** A quantified superiority claim demands the strongest evidence. Twelve subjects is not powered to establish a 40% effect; a court will treat the number as unsubstantiated on its face.
2. **Unpublished + in-house.** Never exposed to scientific discussion, and the independence problem compounds it.
3. **No comparator.** "40% faster" *than what?* Standard gauze? A named competitor? No dressing? An unqualified comparative is misleading under § 5 UWG regardless of the underlying data — and if a competitor is identifiable, § 6 UWG on comparative advertising also engages.
4. **Consistency with your clinical evaluation.** Under MDR Art. 7 claims must not mislead as to performance, and the claim needs to be supported by the clinical evidence in your technical documentation and consistent with the CE intended purpose. Advertising beyond your clinical evaluation is a regulatory exposure on top of the competition-law one. MDR breach also feeds back into § 3a UWG.
5. **§ 3 HWG** applies to Medizinprodukte directly and specifically prohibits attributing a therapeutic efficacy the product does not have.

Germany also has unusually cheap, fast enforcement: an Abmahnung from a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale followed by an einstweilige Verfügung, in forums that are not sympathetic on health claims.

## What I'd do instead

Drop the quantified claim. The realistic alternatives, in descending order of safety:

- Non-quantified performance claims tied to the intended purpose already covered by your clinical evaluation (moist wound healing support, etc.).
- If you want to reference the study at all, qualify it precisely and visibly — but note that accurately describing a methodologically weak study does not rescue it if the ad still presents it as scientific proof of efficacy.
- If the 40% figure matters commercially, treat it as a claim to *earn*: an adequately powered, randomised, controlled, published trial against a defined comparator.

One thing worth checking on your side: whether the 40% figure has already gone into any technical documentation or notified-body submission, because an inconsistency between marketing copy and the clinical evaluation is a worse problem than the copy alone.

I can draft compliant alternative copy against your actual intended purpose wording if you paste the IFU language.

graders.evidence:
I couldn't verify these citations — WebSearch was denied in this session. Everything below is from knowledge, and I've flagged my confidence level per item. **Pull the official text before relying on any Randnummer.**

## First, a framing correction

There is no BGH decision that sets a substantiation standard *specifically for medical devices*. The standard German courts apply to device efficacy claims comes from the BGH's health-related-advertising line, which was developed mainly in pharmaceutical cases and is then applied to Medizinprodukte by the OLGs. If someone hands you a "BGH medical device case," be suspicious.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil vom 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). High confidence on the case, date, docket and name.

The standard it sets, in four parts:

**1. Strengeprinzip.** In health-related advertising, particularly strict requirements apply to the accuracy, unambiguity and clarity of the claim, because errors affect a particularly important legal interest (health).

**2. The methodological benchmark.** A claim of efficacy must rest on *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* at the time of advertising. The BGH's formulation: studies conducted according to the recognised rules of science — in principle a **randomised, placebo-controlled double-blind study with adequate statistical evaluation, which has been brought into the professional discourse through publication**. The four elements are cumulative: randomisation, control, blinding, adequate powering — *plus* publication.

**3. Burden of proof shifts to the advertiser.** Normally the plaintiff proves misleadingness. In health advertising, once the plaintiff shows the claim is scientifically contested or not secured, the advertiser must prove it is substantiated. If the advertiser presents the claim as scientifically proven, they carry the burden outright.

**4. Timing.** The substantiation must exist *when the ad runs*. You cannot cure an unsubstantiated claim with a study completed afterwards. (Roots in **BGH GRUR 1991, 848 – "Rheumalind II"** — medium confidence on the citation.)

Follow-up worth checking: **BGH, Urt. v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"**, which restates the standard. Medium confidence on the docket number.

**The one qualification that matters to you:** the gold standard is "in principle," not absolute. Where a placebo-controlled double-blind trial is genuinely impossible or unethical in the field, other evidence meeting that field's recognised scientific rules can suffice — but the advertiser must show *why* the gold standard is unattainable and that what they have meets the field's actual standard. Wound dressings are a real case for this (blinding a dressing is hard). This qualification is developed mostly in the instance courts, so treat it as an argument to build, not a safe harbour.

## Applied to your facts

n=12, in-house, unpublished fails on nearly every prong simultaneously — sample size, independence, publication, and almost certainly control and blinding. Under Basisinsulin this is not *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis*, and because the burden sits on you, there is no version of the litigation where you win on the evidence.

Two aggravating features specific to your copy:

- **"40% faster" is a quantified claim.** A precise number signals precise evidence. n=12 will not support a point estimate to that resolution, and the gap between the stated precision and the actual evidence is itself the misleadingness.
- **Faster *than what?*** The reference point is unstated. If it reads as a comparison to competitor products, §6 UWG comparative-advertising requirements engage on top. If it reads as "vs. no dressing," that is arguably trivial and separately misleading.

## Beyond the BGH

The UWG claim is not the only exposure:

- **§3 HWG** — misleading to attribute a therapeutic efficacy the product does not have. Routed into competition law via **§3a UWG**; **§5 UWG** applies directly.
- **MDR Art. 7** — prohibits claims that mislead as to performance or clinical benefit. Directly applicable, independent of the BGH line.
- **MDR Art. 61 / Annex XIV** — clinical evidence must support the intended purpose *and the claims made*. For Class IIa your notified body has assessed the clinical evaluation. If "40% faster healing" is not within the certified intended purpose and supported in the CER, you have a **regulatory** problem with the Benannte Stelle, not just an advertising one. This is the exposure people usually miss, and it does not go away by softening the ad copy.
- **Enforcement reality:** Wettbewerbszentrale and VSW monitor this space aggressively and move by Abmahnung. Competitors can act under §8(3) UWG. An einstweilige Verfügung can land in weeks.

## Bottom line

The claim is not defensible on this evidence, and I'd advise against running it. The realistic paths are: drop the quantified claim and describe mechanism or properties within your certified intended purpose; or commission a study designed to the Basisinsulin benchmark — adequately powered, controlled, with a pre-specified endpoint matching the claim wording, and published — and align it with the CER before the claim goes live, not after.

Get a German Wettbewerbsrecht specialist to confirm the citations and review the final copy. I'd also flag that the MDR/notified-body angle should be reviewed by regulatory in parallel with legal; they are separate problems with separate remedies.

I couldn't verify these citations — WebSearch is blocked in this session (don't-ask mode). Everything below is from memory. The doctrine I'm confident about; **the docket number you should have counsel confirm before it goes in a file**. And this is orientation, not a legal opinion — you need German competition counsel before this copy ships.

## The leading case

**BGH, "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** — judgment of 6 February 2013, I ZR 62/11, GRUR 2013, 649.

That is the anchor decision for the substantiation standard in health-related advertising. It is not a medical-device case (it concerned an insulin claim), and that matters less than you'd think: the standard is attached to the *health-relatedness of the claim*, not the product's regulatory class. German courts apply it to medical devices routinely, because the HWG covers medical devices and §5 UWG applies regardless.

There is no separate BGH leading case on medical-device efficacy claims specifically. If someone tells you there is, ask them for the docket.

## The standard it set

Three parts, and your copy has to clear all three:

**1. The claim must rest on *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis*** — secured scientific knowledge, not plausible, not promising, not "our data suggest."

**2. The study evidencing it must meet the evidence-based-medicine gold standard.** The operative formula — I'd call this a close paraphrase rather than a verbatim quote, so have counsel pull the actual Randnummer:

> a randomised, placebo-controlled double-blind study, with an adequate number of participants and adequate statistical evaluation, which through publication has been brought into the discussion process of the expert community.

Note the last clause. Publication is not a nice-to-have in this test; it is a constitutive element. The reasoning is that peer exposure is what converts a result into *secured* knowledge.

**3. The advertising may not state the result more strongly or more broadly than the study actually supports.** This is what actually decided *Basisinsulin*: the underlying data existed, but the claim generalised beyond what it established. A methodologically clean study does not license a claim the study didn't make.

## Two procedural points that usually decide these cases

**The burden is on you.** In health advertising German courts reverse the normal allocation: once the claim is challenged, the advertiser carries the Darlegungs- und Beweislast for scientific substantiation. The claimant does not have to disprove 40%.

**You must hold the substantiation at the time you advertise.** Running a proper trial after an Abmahnung lands does not retroactively cure the claim. And if the science is genuinely contested in the field, advertising one side without disclosing the dispute is itself misleading.

## Applied to your facts

"Heals wounds 40% faster," backed by n=12, in-house, unpublished, fails on every prong at once:

- **Unpublished** — fails the discussion-process element outright. This alone is dispositive; nothing else needs to be reached.
- **n=12** — not an adequate number of participants for a quantified effect size. A 40% figure implies a precision that twelve subjects cannot deliver.
- **In-house** — not fatal in itself, but it removes independence at exactly the point where you have no peer scrutiny to substitute for it.
- **"40% faster" than *what*?** The comparator is unstated. If a reader takes it as against competitor dressings, you're additionally in §6 UWG comparative-advertising territory with a much harder evidentiary burden. If it's against untreated wounds or standard care, that has to be on the face of the claim.

My assessment: this claim is not defensible as written, and the gap isn't close enough to be argued down. I'd treat it as un-shippable rather than risky.

## The regulatory overlay, since it's a device

- **Art. 7 MDR** independently bans misleading claims about device performance. German courts treat it as a market-conduct rule under **§3a UWG**, so an Art. 7 breach is directly actionable by competitors — you don't need a regulator to act.
- **§3 HWG** — misleading therapeutic-efficacy advertising. "Heals faster" is squarely a therapeutic efficacy claim.
- Your claims also have to be consistent with the **clinical evaluation** in your technical documentation (Art. 61 / Annex XIV). A marketing claim that outruns your clinical evidence is a notified-body problem at your next Class IIa surveillance audit, not only a UWG problem.

## Realistic paths forward

1. **Drop the number.** Qualitative claims tied to mechanism and supported by your CE clinical evaluation ("supports moist wound healing") sit in a completely different risk class than a quantified comparative effect.
2. **If you want 40%, buy it properly** — adequately powered, randomised, controlled, published. That's the price of the number.
3. **Interim option:** cite the study transparently and narrowly rather than as a headline claim — explicit n, explicit comparator, explicit preliminary status. Weaker, but at least the reader isn't misled about the evidentiary base. Counsel should still sign off; exploratory data in lay-facing advertising carries its own HWG constraints.

One thing worth knowing about the German enforcement environment: this is a self-policing market. The Wettbewerbszentrale and your competitors both have standing under §8 UWG, and a quantified healing claim on a wound dressing is the kind of copy that attracts an Abmahnung quickly. The practical exposure isn't a fine — it's a cease-and-desist with a penalty clause plus a pulped print run.

Worth flagging: docket number unverified, and the gold-standard formula has some judicial softening where an RCT is genuinely infeasible — but that's mostly OLG-level, the burden of showing infeasibility falls on you, and it wouldn't rescue a quantified 40% claim regardless.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: ECG patch trade-press copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous single-lead ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does not apply
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 0 substantiate, 2 verify.

This copy is close to clean. It tracks the intended purpose almost verbatim, carries the supervision condition rather than dropping it, and makes no numeric performance claim it hasn't backed. One population restriction has gone missing; everything else is an open question for the technical file, not a breach.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — borderline, see Why
**Why:** The assessed intended purpose is restricted to **adults**. The copy states the indication with no population qualifier. Limb (d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" — an unqualified indication in front of a cardiology readership that includes paediatric and congenital cardiologists suggests availability for their patients. I'll be straight that this turns on silence rather than affirmative suggestion, which is the weaker end of (d); a stricter reading says an omission isn't a "suggestion". It isn't worth the argument when the fix is one word.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — not curable by evidence. Cured by narrowing the claim, or by an intended purpose that covers paediatric use.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit", the UWG mirror of intended-purpose drift
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "For use in adults under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Duration is a technical specification, not a use. It doesn't expand the intended purpose, and "up to" is properly hedged. But 14 days is the number a competitor's counsel would test first, and nothing I've been given establishes it.
**Evidence needed:** Validated maximum wear duration from the technical file — adhesive wear-time testing, battery life, and signal quality maintained across the full 14 days. If the validation supports 14 days only under specific conditions (skin prep, single patch, no reapplication), "up to" may not carry that on its own.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if 14 days exceeds validated wear duration, or is achievable only under conditions the copy doesn't state
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** No change needed if the file supports 14 days unconditionally. Note the copy also drops "continuous" from the assessed purpose — no breach, but restoring it costs nothing and is the differentiating property.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so no function or property is ascribed under limb (a). Offering data on request to Fachkreise is a legitimate structure, and for a trade-press format it's proportionate. The exposure sits in what arrives when someone requests it.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the data (i) exists in the technical file, (ii) is for this device in its assessed intended use — clinical arrhythmia detection in adults, not bench or algorithm-only validation on a public database, and (iii) is actually furnished on request, promptly, without a sales gate. If the sens/spec figures are per-arrhythmia-type and vary materially (e.g. strong for AF, weaker for others), the unqualified plural "cardiac arrhythmias" plus an undifferentiated data offer is where a § 5(2) no. 1 "Tests" argument would start.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von Tests", if the data supplied is not for the advertised indication and population, or omits essential components such as the reference standard and arrhythmia breakdown
**Call:** Verify

---

### Limb (c) — likely risk: open question, not a finding

The copy is benefit-framed and surfaces no limitation. I'm not raising (c) on that basis, because I can't name a likely risk from the material supplied — and a (c) finding inferred from "it's an ECG patch" would be unfalsifiable.

Worth noting in the copy's favour: it carries "under healthcare professional supervision," which is the principal use condition in the intended purpose. Most benefit-only device copy drops exactly that.

> The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU — specifically whether it records limitations on interpretation, contraindications, or skin-reaction warnings that a reasonable reader of this claim would need. For trade press, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix if one does bite.

### Provisions checked and clear

- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — no guaranteed-success framing. "Detection of" is capability, not outcome certainty.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** `[verified]` — no no-harmful-effects claim.
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** `[verified]` — no claims about the manufacturer.
- **HWG § 11(1)** `[verified]` — does not apply. Audience is Fachkreise. **Caveat:** if this copy is reused on an ungated web page, § 11 nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 reopen, and no. 7 (health improved by use / impaired by non-use) is the one to re-check at that point.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** `[verified]` — no class, CE, or notified-body claim is made, so there is nothing to mis-state.
- **UWG § 6** `[verified]` — no comparison, express or implied.
- **MDR Art. 7(b)** `[verified]` — no false diagnostic impression. "Detection of cardiac arrhythmias ... under healthcare professional supervision" does not imply autonomous diagnosis.

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

Two changes: "in adults" added, "continuous" restored.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear duration; any conditions attached to it | R&D / regulatory — technical file |
| "sensitivity and specificity data" | The dataset itself: device, population, indication, reference standard, per-arrhythmia breakdown | Clinical affairs |
| Response process | Who fulfils "on request", how fast, and what document is sent | Marketing ops |
| Limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or interpretation limitation | Regulatory — IFU |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 nos. 2(a), 2(b), 3(b); § 11(1) scoping sentence for devices — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4; § 6 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

# Device Claims Review: ECG patch trade-press copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class IIa continuous single-lead ECG patch
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword (drafting, not breach), 2 substantiate, 1 OK.

**No breaches identified** against the provisions this review verifies. This copy tracks the intended purpose closely, keeps the supervision condition, and makes no absolute performance claim — the three things device copy most often drops. What's left is substantiation and one narrowing edit.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** The duration is a device characteristic, not a use claim; "up to" is bounded and non-absolute. But the assessed intended purpose is limited to **adults**, and this sentence carries no population. Silence is not a suggestion of paediatric use, so it does not reach MDR Art. 7(d) [verified] on the material supplied — it is a gap worth closing because the fix is free.
**Evidence needed:** Technical documentation supporting 14-day wear (adhesive, battery, electrode signal quality over the full period) — and confirmation that 14 days is the validated maximum, not a best case.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentliche Merkmale … Beschaffenheit") [verified] — if the technical file supports a shorter validated wear time than 14 days.
**Call:** Needs rewording + substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "Single-lead ECG recording **in adults** for up to 14 days."

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so nothing is asserted that could be false on its face. The exposure is scope: sitting next to "detection of cardiac arrhythmias", it implies performance data across arrhythmias generally. If the clinical evidence covers only atrial fibrillation — the common case for single-lead patches — the pairing ascribes a property the device has not demonstrated across the claimed indication.
**Evidence needed:** The performance study behind the figures, and specifically **which arrhythmias it covers**. Also: confirm the data is actually releasable on request (a gated claim that cannot be honoured is its own problem under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Tests").
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified], UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Ergebnisse … von Tests") [verified] — if the data is narrower than the indication as worded.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** If the data is AF-only, name it: "Sensitivity and specificity data for atrial fibrillation detection available on request." If it spans the broader indication, leave as written.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Tracks the assessed intended purpose almost verbatim and retains the supervision condition — the qualifier that most commonly gets dropped in marketing and that drives limb (d) findings. Nothing here suggests home use, self-interpretation, or an unsupervised setting.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

If this runs in German, the German text is the artefact that gets assessed — the translation must preserve both "bei Erwachsenen" and the supervision condition. Draft for native review:

> Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen über bis zu 14 Tage. Zur Anwendung unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal bei der Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen. Daten zu Sensitivität und Spezifität auf Anfrage.

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. For a 14-day adhesive patch the usual candidates are skin reaction and signal-quality loss over the wear period, but I will not raise MDR Art. 7(c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your material. Worth checking against the IFU. For trade-press copy of this length an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix if one is needed at all.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear duration from the technical file | R&D / RA |
| "sensitivity and specificity data" | The study, and its arrhythmia scope vs. the stated indication | Clinical affairs |
| "available on request" | Confirmed process to actually supply it to Fachkreise requesters | Marketing / RA |
| (c) omission | Whether the IFU records a likely risk warranting a pointer | RA |

## Two scoping notes

- **Fachkreise holds only for the trade-press placement.** If this copy is reused on an ungated web page, HWG § 11(1) nos. 7 and 9 [verified] come into scope and the analysis changes. Re-review before repurposing.
- **No certification or class claim is made**, so UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 [verified] are not engaged. If a CE mark, class, or notified-body reference is added to the layout, that needs checking separately.

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3, § 11(1) nos. 7, 9 — `references/hwg.md` [verified] (§ 3 checked, not engaged; § 11 out of scope for this audience)

  2. Is "data available on request" adequate substantiation for a performance reference in German practice, or does the figure itself need to be in the asset?

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy, continuous ECG patch

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous single-lead ECG patch — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; HWG § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

4 items reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 2 substantiate/verify, 1 OK.

**No breaches identified** against the provisions I verify. This copy is unusually disciplined — it tracks the intended purpose almost verbatim, reproduces the supervision condition rather than dropping it, and declines to state performance figures it would then have to defend. The items below are open questions for the technical file plus one scope tightening.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Recording modality matches the assessed intended purpose. Wear duration is a specification, not an indication — it does not extend the intended purpose, so limb (d) is not engaged. "Up to" is correctly framed as a ceiling, not a typical value.
**Evidence needed:** The validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation / IFU. Adhesive and signal-quality validation must support 14 days, not merely "we have seen it last that long".
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentliche Merkmale … Zwecktauglichkeit") — if the validated duration is shorter than 14 days, or if 14 days is a battery figure rather than a validated recording duration.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** None needed if the technical file supports 14 days.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A true statement about data availability is not a performance claim. Offering data on request to Fachkreise is ordinary practice, and stating no figures means there is no figure to be misleading about. § 5(2) no. 1 reaches statements about "Ergebnisse … von Tests" — this makes none.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the data exists in the form the sentence implies, and that its scope matches the preceding sentence. The sentence before says "cardiac arrhythmias" broadly; if the sensitivity/specificity figures cover only certain arrhythmia classes (AF only, say), the adjacency invites a reader to carry a narrow figure across a broad indication.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if the data is narrower than the arrhythmia scope stated immediately above it, or is bench/algorithm validation being offered as clinical performance.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** If the data is arrhythmia-class-specific, say so: "Sensitivity and specificity data for [arrhythmia classes] available on request." Naming the scope is cheap and removes the adjacency problem entirely.

---

**Claim:** Population scope — the copy states no patient population; the assessed intended purpose is restricted to **adults**.
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Limb (d) prohibits *suggesting* uses outside the assessed purpose. Silence on population is not an affirmative suggestion of paediatric use, so I will not call this a breach on the material in front of me. But this is a drafting note worth acting on: reproducing an intended purpose in advertising while dropping one of its restrictions is the standard drift vector, and "in adults" costs one word.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by wording, not data.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — if this text is placed alongside imagery, captions, or case studies featuring non-adult patients, or if sales collateral derived from it discusses paediatric use.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** Insert "in adults" — see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Tracks the assessed intended purpose on all three operative elements — supervision condition, detection function, arrhythmia scope. Limb (b) is not engaged: the phrasing positions the device within a supervised detection workflow rather than as an autonomous diagnostic, which is what the intended purpose describes. Carrying the supervision condition into the advertising rather than leaving it in the IFU is the right call and does real work here.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

## Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation, contraindication, or interpretation caveat. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs in this asset. I'm not going to infer one from the device category — skin reaction, signal loss under motion, arrhythmia classes the algorithm doesn't flag are all plausible for a patch of this type, but inferring a risk and then flagging the copy for omitting it produces an unfalsifiable finding.

Two things make a (c) breach less likely here than in typical benefit-framed copy: the audience is Fachkreise, who read an IFU, and the copy already states the supervision condition, which is the principal control on misinterpretation for a monitoring-only device. Trade-press copy at this length isn't expected to carry patient-facing safety text.

**Check the IFU's limitations and contraindications section.** If it records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix at this length — not a risk paragraph.

## German overlay

**HWG § 3** — clean. No guaranteed-success framing (§ 3 no. 2(a)), no no-harmful-effects claim (§ 3 no. 2(b)), no statement about the manufacturer's credentials or track record (§ 3 no. 3(b)), and no therapeutic effect ascribed that the intended purpose does not carry (§ 3 no. 1). Note that § 3 applies in full to Fachkreise advertising — the audience does not soften it.

**HWG § 11** — does not apply. Cardiology trade press is Fachkreise. **Conditional flag:** if this copy is reused on an ungated web page, in a LinkedIn post, or in any asset a patient can reach, § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 for devices) switches on. The current wording has no no. 7 shape in it, so the reuse risk is low — but re-run the audience anchor before any repurposing rather than assuming the clearance travels.

**UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** — no exposure. The copy makes no claim about class, CE certification, notified-body involvement, or company status. Worth noting because Class IIa copy frequently adds a certification line at layout stage; if one is added, it needs its own check against the certificate scope.

**UWG § 6** — not engaged. No comparison, express or implied. No "unlike conventional Holter" framing, which is the shape this product category usually reaches for and which would trigger the full § 6(2) cumulative test — particularly no. 1 (same intended purpose) and no. 2 (verifiable).

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

One word changed. If the IFU check above turns up a likely risk, append:

> Please refer to the instructions for use.

If the performance data is arrhythmia-class-specific, use instead:

> Single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data for [classes] available on request.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear/recording duration — adhesive and signal quality, not battery life alone | Regulatory / R&D, from the technical documentation |
| "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" | The dataset itself: clinical vs. bench, and which arrhythmia classes it covers | Clinical affairs |
| (c) omission check | IFU limitations and contraindications section — is there a likely risk in line with the intended purpose? | Regulatory |
| Layout-stage additions | Any certification line, class statement, or patient imagery added after copy sign-off | Marketing / design |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 nos. 1, 2(a), 2(b), 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) (scoping: nos. 7–9, 11, 12 for devices; Fachkreise exclusion) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not releasable as written. One blocker (intended-purpose scope), one high-risk claim (`data available on request`), plus several gaps that a competitor's `Abmahnung` under UWG would go straight to. The underlying product story is fine — the copy just needs to be tightened back onto the intended purpose and given real substantiation.

---

## Findings, ranked

**1. Blocker — "in adults" has been dropped.**
Intended purpose: *"...in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional."* Copy: *"For use under healthcare professional supervision..."* No age qualifier. To a cardiologist reading a trade ad, an unqualified indication reads as covering the paediatric population, which is outside the CE-marked intended purpose. That is advertising beyond the intended purpose under **MDR Art. 7** and misleading advertising under **§ 3 HWG** / **§ 3 MPDG**. `bei Erwachsenen` is non-negotiable and must sit in the same sentence as the indication, not in a footnote.

**2. High risk — "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."**
Three problems stacked:

- It implies favourable performance without letting the reader assess it — material information withheld (**§ 5a UWG**), and misleading under **§ 3 HWG** because the impression of proven accuracy is created without `gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis` being shown.
- If you do cite data, **§ 6 HWG** requires author, date of publication and the exact source, quoted faithfully. "On request" is the standard way this goes wrong in German practice: German courts have repeatedly treated data-on-file teasers in `Fachkreise` advertising as `irreführend` precisely because the claim travels further than the citation.
- Sensitivity/specificity *for what*? Against which reference standard (12-lead? Holter? adjudicated core lab?), in which population, for AF only or "arrhythmias" broadly, and episode-level or patient-level? Undifferentiated accuracy figures are not interpretable, and for a `Fachkreise` audience that is itself a weakness.

Fix: either state the numbers with a full citation inline, or delete the sentence entirely. Do not keep the middle option.

**3. Medium — "up to 14 days" needs substantiation and conditions.**
"Up to" claims must reflect what the technical documentation supports under stated conditions, not a best-case bench number. Check specifically that the IFU's maximum wear time *is* 14 days (not 7 with a 14-day battery), and add the qualifying condition as a footnote. If typical achieved wear time in your clinical data is materially lower, the unqualified "up to" is exposed.

**4. Medium — "detection of cardiac arrhythmias" may over-reach two ways.**
First, if your validation covers atrial fibrillation and a limited set of arrhythmias, the unqualified plural implies broader validated detection. Second, mirror the intended purpose's structure: the device *records* ECG *for the purpose of* detection by the clinician. If there is an onboard algorithm, say what it does; if there isn't, avoid phrasing that suggests the patch itself detects.

**5. Medium — missing mandatory-in-practice elements.**
No manufacturer name, no indication of CE status / notified body, no pointer to the IFU for contraindications, warnings and full performance data. None of these is a formal `Pflichtangaben` block (§ 4 HWG is for medicinal products), but their absence is the standard finding in a German device-advertising audit, and the IFU pointer is what keeps the ad from being read as the complete indication. Also confirm the device is CE-marked *now* — pre-certification promotion requires the **MDR Art. 21** non-conformity notice.

**6. Medium — check the digital edition's audience gating.**
`Fachkreise` status under **§ 2 HWG** is what keeps § 11 HWG out of scope. If the trade title's online version is freely accessible, German case law treats it as `Publikumswerbung`, and the lay-advertising restrictions apply to the same copy. Confirm the publisher gates the digital placement, or run a separate lay-compliant version.

**7. Low — language and translation discipline.**
English is tolerated for `Fachkreise` in Germany, but a German version is the safer default. Critically: do **not** freshly translate the intended purpose. Lift the German wording verbatim from the German-language IFU, which § 8 MPDG requires you to have. A translation that drifts from the registered wording recreates finding 1 in a different form.

---

## Suggested revision

**English**

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days.¹
> For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias.
> In [study, n = X patients], [device] detected [atrial fibrillation] with a sensitivity of [X]% and a specificity of [Y]% versus [reference standard]. [Author, journal, year, DOI]
>
> ¹ [Conditions: e.g. at 25 °C, with the supplied adhesive, single application.]
> Please consult the instructions for use for contraindications, warnings and full performance data. [Manufacturer]. CE [NB number].

**German**

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage.¹
> Zur Anwendung bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen. *(→ verbatim aus der deutschen Gebrauchsanweisung übernehmen)*
> In [Studie, n = X] erkannte [Produkt] [Vorhofflimmern] mit einer Sensitivität von [X] % und einer Spezifität von [Y] % gegenüber [Referenzstandard]. [Autor, Zeitschrift, Jahr, DOI]
>
> ¹ [Bedingungen]
> Weitere Angaben zu Gegenanzeigen, Warnhinweisen und Leistungsdaten entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung. [Hersteller]. CE [Benannte Stelle].

If the citable sensitivity/specificity data doesn't exist yet, cut that line and ship the first two sentences plus the footer — the copy is compliant without it and non-compliant with the "on request" version.

---

## Confirm before sign-off

- Does the IFU state 14 days as maximum **wear time**, and under what conditions?
- Which arrhythmias are validated, against which reference standard, and are the figures episode- or patient-level?
- Is the accuracy data published or data-on-file? (Data-on-file changes the recommendation to "cut the line.")
- Is the digital placement `Fachkreise`-gated?

Standard caveat: this is a copy review against MDR Art. 7, HWG, MPDG and UWG as they apply here, not legal advice — your regulatory affairs and German counsel should sign the final text, particularly on the § 6 HWG citation format.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not clearable as written. Two changes are mandatory (adults; the sens/spec teaser), one needs documentary verification (14 days), plus a missing mandatory identification footnote. Nothing here is comparative or superiority-based, which is the good news — the problems are all omission-type.

## Blocking issues

**1. "in adults" has been dropped — MDR Art. 7(1)(d)**

The Zweckbestimmung is limited to adults. Copy that reads "single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days… in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias" with no population limit suggests a use beyond the stated intended purpose, which is exactly what Art. 7(1)(d) prohibits. In a cardiology title, paediatric and adolescent arrhythmia work is a live reader interest, so the omission is not theoretical. This is the single easiest thing to get wrong and the easiest to fix.

**2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" — §6 HWG, §3 HWG, §5a UWG**

This is the riskiest line. It asserts that favourable diagnostic-accuracy evidence exists and invites the reader to infer it is good, while disclosing nothing that can be checked.

- If a reader understands it as a pointer to a study or scientific evaluation — and in a trade-press context they will — §6 Nr. 1 HWG requires the author, the date, and the source to be named in the advertisement itself. "On request" does not satisfy that; the citation has to travel with the claim.
- Sensitivity and specificity are not device-level constants. They differ by arrhythmia (AF vs. pauses vs. NSVT vs. AV block), by reference standard, and by whether the figure describes the algorithm alone or the algorithm plus human over-read. An unqualified reference to "sensitivity and specificity" for a device whose intended purpose says "cardiac arrhythmias" in the plural implies performance across the whole class. If your data are AF-only — which is typical for this device category — the line is misleading under §3 HWG even though it states no number.
- In German health-related advertising the advertiser carries the full substantiation burden from the moment of publication. "Available on request" does not defer it, and it is a familiar Abmahnung target for the Wettbewerbszentrale.

Fix by either stating the figures with their qualifiers, or deleting the line entirely. Deleting is legitimate and safe; a vague promise of data is worse than no mention of data.

**3. "up to 14 days" — verify before publication**

A wear-duration claim is a performance claim and must match the validated maximum in the technical documentation and IFU (adhesive validation, battery, data integrity over the full period). Confirm the CE-marked maximum is 14 days and not, say, 7 with a 14-day variant, or 14 days only under a specific application protocol. If 14 days is conditional, the condition belongs in the copy or a footnote — a bare "bis zu" that most users cannot actually reach is attackable under §5 UWG independently of MDR.

**4. Missing device identification footnote**

There is no product name, manufacturer, class, CE/notified-body number, or pointer to the IFU. The drug-style "Zu Risiken und Nebenwirkungen…" text of §4(3) HWG does not apply to devices, and §4 Pflichtangaben are medicine-specific — so this is not a statutory Pflichtangabe. But MDR Art. 7(1)(c) requires that promotional material not fail to inform of likely risks, and German trade-press practice and most notified bodies' surveillance expectations treat a manufacturer/CE/IFU footnote as the baseline. If the layout shows a CE mark, the four-digit NB number must appear with it for a Class IIa device.

## Secondary points

**Wording drift from the Zweckbestimmung.** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of…" vs. the approved "under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of…". Harmless in meaning, but there is no upside to paraphrasing an intended purpose. Lift it verbatim.

**Publish in German, from the German IFU.** MDR language requirements bind labelling and IFU, not advertising, and English is tolerated toward Fachkreise. But if you run German copy, take the Zweckbestimmung from the German-language IFU rather than back-translating the English — divergence between the ad and the registered wording is what an inspector or competitor will compare.

**Confirm the channel is genuinely Fachkreise.** §2 HWG turns on the audience, not the publisher's self-description. A print cardiology title is fine; the same copy on a freely accessible website or an ungated newsletter becomes Publikumswerbung and pulls in §11 HWG. If a digital placement is planned, gate it.

**"Continuous" was dropped.** A narrowing, so low risk, but it is a genuine product attribute and matches the Zweckbestimmung — keep it.

## Suggested rewrite

German, assuming AF data and a verified 14-day maximum — replace the bracketed fields:

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen, Tragedauer bis zu 14 Tage.¹
>
> Zur Anwendung unter der Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
>
> Sensitivität [XX] % (95 %-KI [XX–XX]), Spezifität [XX] % (95 %-KI [XX–XX]) für die Erkennung von [Vorhofflimmern] gegenüber [Referenzstandard, z. B. simultanem Holter-EKG, adjudiziert durch zwei Kardiologen]; n = [XXX]. [Autor et al., Zeitschrift, Jahr].
>
> ¹ Validierte maximale Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.
>
> [Produktname] — Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. CE [NB-Nr.]. Hersteller: [Name, Anschrift]. Gebrauchsanweisung und Sicherheitshinweise beachten.

If the accuracy data are not yet publishable, cut the third paragraph entirely rather than softening it. The first two paragraphs plus the footnotes stand on their own and are clean.

Two things I cannot check from here: the validated wear duration and which arrhythmias your sens/spec figures actually cover. Both need to come from the technical documentation before this runs — the rewrite is only correct if the bracketed values match it.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Overall

The copy is close, but it doesn't track the intended purpose closely enough in two places, and the performance line is the weakest part. For a Fachkreise audience in Germany the governing frame is MDR Art. 7 (prohibition on misleading claims), § 3 HWG (Irreführungsverbot — applies regardless of audience) and §§ 5/5a UWG. The audience restriction helps you: § 11 HWG (Laienwerbung) largely falls away, so specifics are permitted and in fact expected. The practical enforcement risk here is a competitor Abmahnung or Wettbewerbszentrale complaint, not BfArM.

## Findings, most serious first

**1. "In adults" has been dropped.** The intended purpose is restricted to adults; the copy is silent on population. Silence in a cardiology trade ad reads as "unrestricted," and a paediatric/adolescent reader has no cue that this is off-label. This is the clearest MDR Art. 7 exposure in the piece — an omission that broadens the indication. Restore it.

**2. The sensitivity/specificity line may imply a function the intended purpose doesn't grant.** The intended purpose is *recording* "for the detection of" arrhythmias — it does not say the device detects or classifies them. Quoting sensitivity and specificity implies an automated detection algorithm whose diagnostic performance is the product's. If the device records and a physician interprets, that's scope creep; if there *is* a cleared detection algorithm inside the Class IIa scope, then say so explicitly and attribute the figures to it. Either way, undifferentiated "sensitivity and specificity" is close to meaningless — sensitivity for AF is not sensitivity for pauses, VT or AV block. Name the arrhythmia, the reference standard, N, and the population.

**3. "Up to 14 days" needs to match the IFU, not the best case.** Two checks: (a) the maximum validated wear time in the technical documentation and IFU must be 14 days — adhesive, battery, signal quality over the full period; (b) German case law treats "bis zu" as a figure typical users actually reach, not a lab ceiling. If real-world median wear is 7 days, "up to 14" is attackable even if 14 is technically validated.

**4. "Data available on request" is substantiation-by-promise.** It's not per se unlawful for Fachkreise, but it creates two risks: an Irreführung durch Unterlassen argument under § 5a UWG (material information withheld at the point of the claim), and an operational one — if the request is slow-walked, or what arrives is bench/algorithm-only data rather than clinical data on this device, the original claim was unsupported when made. Also note § 6 HWG: the moment you reference a study or expert opinion, you must name the source. Better to publish the figures with a citation. Fachkreise readers discount unquantified performance claims anyway.

**5. Minor: "continuous" was dropped, and the device isn't identified as a medical device.** "Continuous" is in your intended purpose and is a genuine differentiator — keep it. Adding a Class IIa / CE and an IFU pointer isn't strictly mandated for a Fachkreise ad (the § 4 HWG Pflichtangaben catalogue is drug-specific), but many German publishers expect it and it's cheap insurance.

**6. Language.** Market is Germany but the copy is English. Advertising language isn't itself regulated, but the German IFU and Declaration of Conformity are authoritative — the German intended-purpose wording must be lifted verbatim, not re-translated from the English ad.

## Suggested revision

EN:

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use in adults, under the supervision of a healthcare professional, for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. In [study, N=___], the [device/algorithm] detected [AF / specified arrhythmias] with a sensitivity of __% and a specificity of __% versus [reference standard]. [Full citation.] [Product] is a CE-marked Class IIa medical device. Please refer to the instructions for use.

DE (pull the second sentence verbatim from the German Zweckbestimmung rather than using mine):

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage. Zur Anwendung bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen. In [Studie, n=___] betrugen Sensitivität __% und Spezifität __% gegenüber [Referenzstandard]. [Quelle.] Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung.

## What I'd need from you to sign this off

The IFU's stated maximum wear time; whether the Class IIa scope includes an automated detection/classification algorithm or recording only; and the source of the sensitivity/specificity figures (clinical study on this device vs. algorithm validation on a public database). Findings 2 and 3 can't be closed without those.

# Device Claims Review: French consumer web page

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum / grand public — ungated consumer web page
**Markets:** France only (EU layer applies; German overlay switched off)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed, and one claim needs a French-law check I can't perform.

## Scope — read this before the findings

Stripping the German overlay removes the two provisions that would have caught this copy fastest: HWG § 11(1) no. 7 (health impaired by *not* using the device) for the fear appeal, and HWG § 11(1) no. 11 plus § 3 no. 3(b) for the named-clinician endorsement. Those are gone. Don't read their absence as the copy being safer — it means the analysis now rests on MDR Art. 7 alone plus French national rules, and **French national advertising rules for medical devices are outside what this skill verifies.**

France regulates public-facing device advertising in the Code de la santé publique (the L.5213-x series, with ANSM as the competent authority), and that regime is generally understood to restrict references to recommendations by health professionals in advertising aimed at the public, and to require specified mandatory wording. `[verify]` — I am naming that as a pointer, not citing it. I have not read the text, this skill does not verify it, and I will not state what it requires. Your single highest-value next step is putting the endorsement sentence in front of someone who can read that regime properly.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur — mesurez votre tension chaque jour."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The sentence links not-measuring to cardiac jeopardy and measuring to protection, which is "creating a false impression regarding treatment" — a monitoring device that reports a blood-pressure value delivers no cardiac outcome. This is the outcome-implication-from-a-monitoring-only-device shape.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. No dataset makes a measurement device protect a heart. Cured by rewording only.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — dormant while the copy stays out of Germany. If this page is ever translated for DE or becomes reachable from a DE-targeted campaign, this sentence is the first thing to pull.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Read separately from the fear framing, this is a use-frequency instruction addressed to an undifferentiated public. Whether it drifts outside the assessed intended purpose depends entirely on that purpose — a monitor assessed for self-monitoring by people with diagnosed or suspected hypertension, on a schedule set by a clinician, is not the same device as one telling everybody to measure daily.
**Evidence needed:** the intended purpose as assessed, and any measurement protocol in the IFU.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose names an indicated population or a clinician-directed measurement schedule, this sentence suggests a use outside it. That is the limb this copy is most likely to fail, and I can't close it without the anchor.
**Call:** Needs rewording (provisionally — confirm against intended purpose)

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none identifiable under MDR Art. 7 `[verified]`
**Why:** An endorsement attached to no specific capability claim doesn't by itself ascribe a function the device lacks (limb a) or state a diagnostic property (limb b). Art. 7 is not the provision that governs this.
**Evidence needed:** written consent from the named individual; confirmation the title and specialty are accurate as stated; disclosure status of any commercial relationship.
**Also engaged:** French CSP/ANSM public-advertising rules `[verify]` — out of scope here, and the reason this claim can't clear on my review. Separately, HWG § 3 no. 3(b) and UWG § 5(2) if the copy ever reaches Germany.
**Call:** Verify — and do not publish this sentence on the strength of an Art. 7 review, because Art. 7 is not where its risk lives.

## Paste-ready copy

**Option A — endorsement removed (publishable without waiting on the French-law check):**

> Suivez votre tension artérielle à domicile. Mesurez-la à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin et présentez-lui vos relevés. Un relevé de tension ne remplace pas un diagnostic médical.

**Option B — endorsement retained, only if French counsel clears it:** keep Option A's three sentences and append the endorsement with the commercial relationship stated, e.g. `Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue, consultant rémunéré par [Société].` Don't ship this variant on my say-so.

Both drop "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" entirely rather than softening it — the sentence has no compliant version, because its whole function is the implication that breaches (b). Both also replace the universal daily instruction with a clinician-set frequency, which keeps the "use it regularly" intent while removing the (d) exposure.

## Open question I could not resolve

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — misinterpretation of readings without clinical context is the obvious candidate for a home monitor sold to the general public, but I'm not raising Art. 7(c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your documentation. Check the IFU; if it records one, the fix is a pointer in the copy, not a redesign of it. Option A's third sentence is drafted to carry that pointer if you need it to.

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" | Intended purpose as assessed + IFU measurement protocol | Regulatory affairs / technical file |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | French CSP/ANSM position on health-professional recommendations in public device advertising | French regulatory counsel |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Written consent, title accuracy, commercial relationship disclosure | Marketing / legal |
| Whole page | Any mandatory French wording for public device advertising | French regulatory counsel |

It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

Web search is blocked in this session, so I couldn't confirm the exact article numbers against Légifrance. The substance below I'm confident in; I've marked the pin cites that should be verified before this goes to your regulatory function.

## Verdict: do not publish. Two blocking violations.

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited endorsement

French law bans public-facing medical device advertising from invoking a recommendation by scientists, health professionals, or people whose notoriety could encourage use. This is the DM analogue of the medicines rule at R.5122-4 CSP; for devices it sits in the R.5213-* series (I believe **R.5213-4 CSP**, introduced by décret n° 2012-743 — *verify the number*). A named cardiologue endorsing a BP monitor is the paradigm case the provision exists to catch. There is no "but he really does recommend it" defence; truthfulness is irrelevant to this prohibition.

Worth flagging separately: if Prof. Dubois is a real identifiable physician, he carries his own exposure under the code de déontologie médicale (R.4127-13 and the bar on lending medical authority to commercial promotion). Using his name puts a clinician at personal risk, not just you.

**Note on your scoping.** France-only doesn't rescue this. The endorsement ban is often mentally filed as a German HWG §11 issue — France has its own, independently applicable. Removing Germany from scope changes nothing here.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited fear appeal

Public DM advertising may not suggest that the subject's health could be affected by *not* using the device. "Don't gamble with your heart" does exactly that: it frames non-purchase as cardiac risk. Same article as above. It also cuts against the general requirement that advertising present the device objectively and promote its *bon usage*.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — likely non-compliant, and clinically off

Two problems. First, this is a usage instruction that almost certainly doesn't match your IFU — check it. Second, it contradicts the established French self-measurement protocol: the *règle des 3* (3 measurements morning, 3 evening, 3 consecutive days ahead of a consultation), per HAS/CFLHTA. Advertising a daily-forever regimen promotes use inconsistent with the recognised protocol, which is squarely the *bon usage* problem, and unsupervised daily self-monitoring is a known driver of anxiety and unnecessary consultations. Fix this even if you didn't have to.

### 4. Missing mandatory mentions

The copy carries none of the required elements for public DM advertising. You need at minimum:

- device name and its **destination** (intended purpose)
- manufacturer or EU authorised representative
- « Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. »
- an invitation to read the instructions — « Lisez attentivement la notice. »

Exact wording and placement rules are in the ANSM *recommandations relatives à la publicité pour les dispositifs médicaux*; pull the current version rather than copying mine verbatim.

## What's fine

- **Class IIa is eligible** for public advertising without gating (L.5213-3 CSP permits classes I and IIa; IIb/III only via the arrêté list). Your no-gating premise holds.
- Class IIa is the right classification for a non-invasive BP monitor under MDR Rule 10.

## Verify before publishing

- Whether home BP monitors appear on the arrêté listing DM "présentant un risque important" that require **ANSM prior authorisation (visa PP)** for public advertising. My recollection is they do not, but I couldn't check and a wrong answer here is a pre-publication blocker, not a copy edit.
- Article numbers in §1–2 above against Légifrance.
- Your IFU's stated measurement frequency.

## Suggested replacement

> **[Nom du produit]** — tensiomètre électronique de bras pour la mesure de la pression artérielle à domicile.
>
> Suivez votre tension chez vous et partagez vos résultats avec votre médecin. Pour un suivi fiable, appliquez la règle des 3 : 3 mesures le matin, 3 le soir, 3 jours de suite avant votre consultation.
>
> Fabricant : [Nom].
> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. L'automesure ne remplace pas le suivi médical.

This drops the endorsement, replaces the fear appeal with the actual benefit (data you bring to your doctor), and aligns the usage instruction with the recognised protocol. The clinical-authority framing you were buying with "Professeur Dubois" is better served by citing an ESH/protocol validation of the device itself, if it has one — that's a factual performance claim about the product and is permitted, whereas a person's endorsement is not.

## Verdict: do not publish as written

Two of the three elements in this copy are, as far as I can tell, independently prohibited in French public-facing medical device advertising, and the third is a clinical-accuracy problem. This needs a rewrite, not a tweak.

---

## Findings

**1. The named-professor endorsement — prohibited (high severity)**

French rules on advertising medical devices to the public (Code de la santé publique, art. L.5213-1 et seq. and the implementing R.5213 articles, mirroring the medicines regime at R.5122-4) prohibit public advertising that refers to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or persons whose notoriety could encourage use of the device. ANSM's guidance on DM advertising calls out health-professional testimonials specifically. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" is the paradigm case — title, specialty, and named authority all doing exactly the work the rule forbids.

Three further problems stack on top, each sufficient on its own:
- **If Prof. Dubois is not a real consenting person**, this is a fabricated endorsement → misleading commercial practice under Code de la consommation art. L.121-2, with DGCCRF exposure.
- **If he is real**, the French medical code of ethics (art. R.4127-13 CSP) bars physicians from lending their name to commercial promotion — so his own ordinal exposure makes participation unlikely to be lawful for him.
- **If he's compensated**, the transparency-of-links regime (L.1453-1) and the anti-cadeaux rules (L.1453-3 et seq.) both engage.

There is no disclosure or disclaimer that rescues this. Remove it.

**2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited fear appeal (high severity)**

Public DM advertising must not suggest that the person's health could be harmed by *not* using the device, and must not use alarming or fear-inducing representations. "Don't gamble with your heart" is a direct implication of cardiac risk from non-purchase. It also arguably misleads about intended purpose under MDR art. 7 (directly applicable in France): a BP monitor measures; it does not protect your heart.

**3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — clinically wrong and likely off-label (medium-high)**

French/European self-measurement guidance (HAS, ESH — the *règle des 3*) is three measurements morning and evening over three consecutive days ahead of a consultation, not indefinite daily monitoring by the general public. Unsupervised daily measurement is not recommended for unselected consumers and is associated with health anxiety. Two consequences:
- If the device's IFU/intended purpose doesn't specify daily use, this is promotion beyond intended purpose (MDR art. 7).
- Directing the public on measurement frequency substitutes for medical advice, which public DM advertising must not do.

**4. Missing mandatory mentions (high severity — blocks publication regardless of the above)**

Public advertising for a medical device must carry, per R.5213-1 CSP and ANSM's recommendation:
- the device's trade name;
- its intended purpose (*destination*);
- the CE-marking statement and express invitation to read the instructions — conventionally: *"Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice."*;
- manufacturer identification;
- reimbursement status where relevant.

The submitted copy has none of these. **Verify the exact current mandatory wording against ANSM's published recommendation before sign-off** — I'm working from recall on the precise phrasing, and it has been revised.

**5. Typo:** `coeur` → `cœur`.

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **Suivez votre tension artérielle à la maison.**
>
> [Nom du produit] est un autotensiomètre électronique destiné à la mesure de la pression artérielle au bras chez l'adulte.
>
> Votre médecin ou votre pharmacien vous indiquera à quelle fréquence effectuer vos mesures et comment interpréter vos résultats.
>
> *[Nom du produit] est un dispositif médical de classe IIa, marqué CE. Fabricant : [X]. Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. [Date de rédaction]*

This keeps the commercial intent (home monitoring, daily-life framing) while routing frequency guidance back to a health professional, which is where the regulator wants it.

---

## Before sign-off

1. **Prior authorisation (visa PP):** confirm whether autotensiomètres appear on the arrêté list of devices whose public advertising requires ANSM prior authorisation under L.5213-4. My understanding is that the list targets higher-risk categories and that a Class IIa home BP monitor falls outside it — but confirm against the current arrêté rather than taking that from me.
2. **Reimbursement status:** if this model is taken in charge by assurance maladie even partially, the public-advertising restriction at L.5213-3 may apply and changes the analysis materially.
3. **IFU cross-check:** the final claim set must sit inside the declared intended purpose.
4. Whatever the origin of the Prof. Dubois line, find out — if a real clinician was approached or engaged, that relationship needs reviewing independently of this copy.

One note despite the France-only scope: if this ever gets reused in Germany, §11 HWG bans professional endorsements and fear-based appeals in public advertising too, so the rewrite above is the safer asset to have on file either way.
