## Verdict

Don't ship this. The first sentence is very likely a hard legal prohibition in France, not a tone problem, and the second is a fear appeal plus an unsupported usage instruction. Both halves need to go.

---

## 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited

French advertising rules for medical devices (Code de la santé publique, the L.5213-x / R.5213-x series) carry the same prohibition as the medicines regime: public-facing advertising may not refer to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or persons whose celebrity could encourage use of the device. A named cardiologist with a *Professeur* title (a regulated hospital-university rank in France) is the paradigm case — the title actively aggravates it by adding institutional authority.

I'm confident about the substance of this rule; I'd have counsel pin the exact article number before you cite it internally, since the DM articles were renumbered when the MDR implementing ordinance landed.

Three knock-on problems even if you somehow got past the main ban:

- **The physician's own exposure.** Code de déontologie médicale (R.4127-13 and the surrounding articles) bars a doctor from lending their name to a commercial product or giving public communications a promotional character. You'd be putting Dubois in front of the Ordre, not just your own file.
- **Transparency.** If there's any payment, contract, or benefit behind the recommendation, it's a declarable link under the French Sunshine regime (L.1453-1) and the undisclosed endorsement is independently an unfair commercial practice under Code de la consommation L.121-2 et seq.
- **Substantiation.** "Recommandé par" is a factual claim needing a signed, dated recommendation on file plus verified credentials. Do you have that document? Marketing teams frequently have an email.

**Fix:** delete. There's no disclosure or asterisk that rescues it — the prohibition is on the reference itself, not on undisclosed references. No gating on the page means you also can't argue HCP-only audience.

## 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — fear appeal

Advertising must not suggest the reader's health will suffer if they don't use the product. This line does exactly that, and it does something worse: it implies that measuring prevents cardiac events. A Class IIa sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure. It doesn't protect a heart. That's a benefit claim beyond intended purpose and runs into MDR Article 7, which prohibits text creating a false impression regarding the device's therapeutic or diagnostic function.

(Also: `coeur` → `cœur`.)

## 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — unsupported clinical instruction

This is you, the manufacturer, issuing a measurement protocol. Two problems:

- Daily indefinite self-measurement is not the standard protocol. ESH/ESC guidance for home monitoring is structured 7-day series (morning and evening, duplicate readings) around a diagnostic or follow-up window — not perpetual daily use. So the line is clinically off.
- If it's not in your IFU, promoting it is promotion of a use outside the approved intended purpose.

**Fix:** hand the frequency decision back to the prescriber — "selon les recommandations de votre médecin."

## 4. Missing mandatory elements

Regardless of what you replace the copy with, French public DM advertising must carry the device designation, its intended purpose, the CE/regulated-product statement, and an instruction to read the notice. Standard wording:

> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. Fabricant : [X].

---

## Suggested replacement

> **Tensiomètre [Marque – Modèle]** — automesure de la pression artérielle à domicile.
> Mesurez votre tension chez vous et partagez vos résultats avec votre médecin, selon ses recommandations.
> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. Fabricant : [X].

Objective, states intended purpose, keeps the clinical decision with the physician, carries the mandatory mentions.

---

## Two things to confirm before publishing

1. **Visa PP.** Prior ANSM authorisation applies to the device categories set by arrêté — generally Class IIb/III, so a Class IIa monitor probably doesn't need one. Confirm your model isn't on the list.
2. **Reimbursement status.** If the device is on the LPPR / taken in charge by assurance maladie, public advertising is prohibited outright. Home BP monitors usually aren't, but check yours.

---

Two smaller notes, since you scoped the market deliberately. A public French-language page with no gating is readable from Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Quebec whatever the commercial market definition says — worth knowing your risk surface isn't strictly territorial. And if this copy is ever proposed for reuse in Germany, the HCP endorsement fails there too under HWG §11(1) — so the fixed version is the one worth putting in the reusable library.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: congress booth panel copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

One claim breaches on the material in front of me: **"Approved"**. The rest are not misleading on what I have, but three of them rest on facts I have not seen.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Approved and available now." — the word **"Approved"**
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]` — "Aussagen oder Symbole, die ... sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen"
**Why:** There is no approval or *Zulassung* regime for medical devices in the EU. A Class IIb device reaches the market through conformity assessment and CE marking, not through an authorisation decision. "Approved", unqualified and with no authority named, is an Angabe about regulatory status that is *zur Täuschung geeignet* — and in a German booth context it maps onto "zugelassen", the medicinal-product word. The § 5(1) materiality filter is comfortably met: regulatory status is exactly what an interventional cardiologist at a booth makes a purchasing or trial decision on.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — not curable by evidence. The device genuinely holds a CE certificate; the fix is to say what it actually holds.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 3 — if the copy elsewhere attributes the "approval" to the company rather than the goods.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under MDR (Class IIb), notified body [NB number]."

---

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Unqualified coverage language with two available readings — full *length* of the treated lesion, or uniform circumferential distribution. Neither is anchored to a size range. If the IFU restricts lesion length or reference vessel diameter, the claim as written suggests fitness for lesions outside the assessed range.
**Evidence needed:** The IFU's lesion length and reference vessel diameter range; the elution data showing drug distribution across the stented segment.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and (d) `[verified]`, UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — **if** the IFU limits lesion length or diameter, or if the distribution data does not cover the full stented segment. (d) cannot be confirmed without the intended purpose.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "across the stented segment, in lesions of [X–Y] mm in vessels of [A–B] mm" — bound it to the assessed range rather than to "the full lesion". Note the cure path differs: if this turns out to be a (d) problem, more data will not fix it; only narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment will.

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A performance claim about the device's own function, which is what a DES does. "Sustained" carries no duration, so nothing in it is false — but nothing in it is checkable either. Under UWG's economics, a broad unverifiable claim is expensive to defend even when true; a narrow figure is cheap.
**Evidence needed:** Elution kinetics from the technical documentation — release profile and duration, with the study or bench method behind it.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a), HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]` — if the elution data does not support "sustained" as a Fachkreis reader would understand it.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "sustained sirolimus release over [X] days (see elution profile, [study/data ref])"

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Availability is expressly a *wesentliches Merkmal* under § 5(2) no. 1. Accurate if true.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation the device is actually on the German market now, and that the full size matrix shown at the booth is orderable — not just part of it.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Verfügbarkeit") — if only some sizes ship, or German market entry is pending.
**Call:** Verify

---

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU. I'm not raising (c) as a finding: the skill's discipline is that the risk must come from supplied material, and inferring one from "it's a coronary stent" would make the finding unfalsifiable. Trade-show copy for Fachkreise is also not expected to carry patient-facing safety text — where (c) does bite on an asset this short, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix, which the revised copy below includes anyway.

## Paste-ready revised copy

**English:**

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent is designed for sustained sirolimus release over [X] days across the stented segment, in lesions of [X–Y] mm. CE marked under MDR — Class IIb, notified body [NB number]. Available in Germany now.
> Please consult the instructions for use for indications, sizing and contraindications.

**German (booth panels for a German congress are usually German — check which language ships):**

> Unser Sirolimus-freisetzender Stent ist auf eine kontinuierliche Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage im gestenteten Segment ausgelegt, bei Läsionen von [X–Y] mm. CE-Kennzeichnung nach MDR — Klasse IIb, Benannte Stelle [NB-Nummer]. Ab sofort in Deutschland verfügbar.
> Angaben zu Indikationen, Größen und Kontraindikationen entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung.

Fill the brackets from the technical documentation. If a bracket can't be filled, delete the phrase rather than restoring the vaguer wording.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "sustained drug release" | Elution kinetics: release profile and duration, with study/bench reference | R&D / technical documentation owner |
| "across the full lesion" | IFU lesion length and reference vessel diameter range; drug distribution across stented segment | RA / clinical affairs |
| "Approved" | CE certificate: NB number, scope, expiry | RA |
| "available now" | German market availability confirmation, full size matrix | Commercial / supply chain |
| limb (c) | IFU contraindications, warnings, DAPT requirements — does a likely risk belong on this panel? | RA / clinical affairs |

## Not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c). "Across the full lesion" is the phrase most likely to turn into a (d) finding once the intended purpose is on the table.

## Two audience caveats

- I've taken **Fachkreise** at face value on your account of the setting. Congress booths inside a delegate-badged hall are Fachkreise; if the hall has open public or press access, or the panel photograph goes onto an ungated website, HWG § 11 switches on for devices — nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 only. No. 7 (health improved by use / impaired by non-use) is the one this copy's framing would meet first.
- Reusing this copy on the public site is a separate review, not a copy-paste.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) (scoping note, nos. 7–9, 11, 12 for devices) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: Congress booth panel copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed** (see end)
**Audience:** Fachkreise — interventional cardiologists at a congress booth. HWG § 11 does **not** apply. HWG § 3 does. [verified]
**Markets:** DE (EU layer + German overlay both apply)

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 2 verify, 1 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

Headline: two rewording items — "across the full lesion" and "Approved" — plus two items to check against the technical file and the commercial launch status.

---

## Findings

### 1. "across the full lesion"

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release **across the full lesion**"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — *Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit, von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse* [verified]
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". A stent elutes drug across **the segment it covers**, which is a function of the device length the operator selects and deploys — not a property of the device that holds for any lesion. As written, the phrase asserts complete lesion coverage unconditionally, which the device cannot deliver independently of sizing.
**Evidence needed:** Cannot be cured by evidence at this wording. The available lengths/diameters and the sizing instruction are in the IFU; the claim needs to be tied to the stented segment instead.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose specifies lesion-length or vessel-diameter ranges, "full lesion" reads as a suggestion of use outside them. Cannot be confirmed until the intended purpose is supplied.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "…sustained drug release across the stented segment."

### 2. "Approved"

**Claim:** "**Approved** and available now."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 — "Aussagen oder Symbole, die [...] sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen" [verified]
**Why:** The device's status is genuine — CE marked with a notified body involved — so this is not a false-certificate case. The problem is the word. In the German market "Zulassung/approved" is the vocabulary of an authority marketing authorisation; a device undergoes a **conformity assessment** and carries a CE marking. An unqualified "Approved" is an *zur Täuschung geeignete Angabe* about the nature of the status, and status drives purchasing decisions, so the § 5(1) materiality filter is met. The fix is free: you hold a stronger, more specific fact than the vague word conveys.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by naming the actual status. Pull the NB number and certificate scope from the DoC.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under MDR (Class IIb, notified body [NB number])."

### 3. "sustained drug release"

**Claim:** "delivers **sustained** drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A release-kinetics claim is legitimate for a DES and is exactly what the elution data in the technical file exists to support. It is not misleading on the material supplied.
**Evidence needed:** The elution profile from the technical documentation. Check that "sustained" matches the assessed profile and, if the file supports a duration, state it — a specific number is cheap to defend under an Abmahnung, a broad adjective is expensive even when true.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — *Tests* (results and essential components of tests), if the duration ultimately cited comes from bench or clinical data presented selectively.
**Call:** Verify

### 4. "available now"

**Claim:** "Approved and **available now**."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Availability is not misleading on the material supplied.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the stent is actually orderable in Germany, in the sizes shown at the booth, on the day the panel is displayed.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — **Verfügbarkeit** is named expressly as a *wesentliches Merkmal* [verified]. If the device is CE marked but not yet shipping in DE, or only some sizes are, this becomes a breach.
**Call:** Verify

### 5. "Our sirolimus-eluting stent"

**Claim:** "Our **sirolimus-eluting** stent"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A composition statement. Accurate composition is unobjectionable; HWG § 3 no. 3(a) (*unwahre Angaben über die Zusammensetzung oder Beschaffenheit*) [verified] would only bite if the drug or the elution mechanism were misstated.
**Call:** OK

---

## Open question — limb (c), risk omission

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation or contraindication. MDR Art. 7(c) is an **omission** test: copy containing nothing false can still breach it by "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose" [verified].

I am not raising (c) as a breach, because I have not seen your IFU and the risk has to come from supplied material rather than from what I assume about the device category. **Worth checking against the IFU** — if it records a likely risk attaching to use in line with the intended purpose, this panel currently carries nothing about it.

Booth-panel length is context here. A trade-show panel is not expected to carry patient-facing safety text, and the proportionate fix where (c) genuinely bites is a pointer, not a paragraph:

> "Please refer to the Instructions for Use for indications, sizing and contraindications."

Adding that line is cheap and closes the question either way. I would add it.

---

## Paste-ready revision

> "Our sirolimus-eluting stent delivers sustained drug release across the stented segment. CE marked under MDR (Class IIb, notified body [NB number]) — available in Germany now.
> Please refer to the Instructions for Use for indications, sizing and contraindications."

If the technical file supports a specific duration, replace "sustained" with it: "…delivers controlled drug release over [X] days across the stented segment."

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "sustained drug release" | Elution profile; confirm the adjective (or a stated duration) matches the assessed release kinetics | Regulatory / R&D — technical documentation |
| "CE marked … Class IIb, NB [number]" | Certificate number, NB identification number, certificate scope | Regulatory — Declaration of Conformity |
| "available now" | DE commercial availability on the congress dates, and which sizes | Sales / supply chain |
| Limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose | Regulatory — IFU |
| Limb (d) | The intended purpose **as assessed** | Regulatory — technical documentation / DoC |

---

## Not engaged

- **HWG § 11** — audience is Fachkreise. § 11 applies only outside professional circles. Not applied. [verified]
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** (*Erfolg mit Sicherheit*) — "delivers" asserts a device function, not certainty of a clinical outcome. Not engaged on this wording. [verified]
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** (no harmful effects) — the copy makes no safety-reassurance claim. [verified]
- **UWG § 6** — no comparison, express or implied. No competitor is *erkennbar*. [verified]
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only; does not apply to devices. [verified]

---

## Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

Two things above hinge on it: "across the full lesion" (finding 1), and whether anything else on the booth panel — images, the stent diagram, the caption, the sizing chart — suggests a vessel, lesion type or patient population outside the assessed scope. Send me the full panel and the intended purpose together and I will close both.

---

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified] |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(a), no. 2(b), no. 3(a); § 3a; § 11(1) | `references/hwg.md` [verified] |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1, no. 4; § 6 | `references/uwg.md` [verified] |

---

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: congress booth panel

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — stated Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 does not apply [verified]
**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply cumulatively)

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 2 substantiate, 2 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Approved"
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] — "Aussagen oder Symbole, die [...] sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen"
**Why:** The device holds a CE marking following conformity assessment with notified body involvement. It does not hold an "approval" in the sense of a *Zulassung*. "Approved", and still more its natural German rendering "zugelassen", points at the medicinal-product authorisation regime and overstates the regulatory status the device actually has. § 5(2) no. 4 reaches statements about the authorisation status of the goods independently of whether the performance claims are accurate.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — not cured by evidence. Cured by naming the actual status.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(a) [verified] if a German version reads "zugelassen"; that is an Angabe about the Beschaffenheit of the product capable of deceiving.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE-marked" / "CE-gekennzeichnet" — with the certificate holder and notified body number on the panel if you want the notified-body involvement to carry weight.

---

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Stated unconditionally, this asserts drug delivery over the entire lesion irrespective of sizing. A stent delivers across the segment it spans; coverage of the full lesion is a function of correct length selection, not a property of the device. If the technical documentation does not support uniform elution over the stented segment, or if the available length matrix cannot span the lesion lengths the panel implies, this becomes MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] — ascribing a property the device does not have — and HWG § 3 no. 1 [verified].
**Evidence needed:** Elution-uniformity data along the stent length from the technical file; the available length matrix; the wording the intended purpose uses about lesion length.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "across the stented segment" — accurate, narrow, and cheap to defend. A verifiable narrow claim is the one that survives an Abmahnung; a broad one is expensive even when true.

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** "Sustained" carries no duration. For a Fachkreise audience at a booth this is a recognised class descriptor rather than a performance figure, so it is not misleading on its face — but § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] covers "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse", and an unqualified release claim invites the cardiologist to supply their own number.
**Evidence needed:** Release-kinetics data and the release period stated in the technical documentation.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] if the release profile in the technical file is materially shorter than the audience would infer.
**Call:** Verify — then state the period.
**Suggested fix:** "sustained sirolimus release over [X] days" — a stated number is both stronger at a booth and safer.

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Availability is expressly an essential characteristic under § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] ("Verfügbarkeit"). No issue if it is true for Germany at the time the booth is staffed.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation that the full advertised size matrix is orderable in Germany on the congress dates, and that the CE certificate scope covers every size on display.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] if any displayed size or configuration sits outside the certificate scope.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** Keep, or narrow to "available in Germany from [date]" if any sizes are staged.

---

**Claim:** "Our sirolimus-eluting stent"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Factual composition descriptor. HWG § 3 no. 3(a) [verified] would bite only if the eluted substance were not sirolimus.
**Call:** OK

---

## Two things I could not assess

**Limb (d) — not assessed.** Suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I have not seen the intended purpose. Paste it from the technical documentation or the DoC and I will cover it — in particular whether "full lesion" sits inside the lesion-length and vessel-diameter wording the conformity assessment covered. This limb is usually **not** curable by data; it is cured by narrowing the claim.

**Limb (c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I cannot tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs on this panel. Worth checking against the IFU. Trade-press and booth copy is not expected to carry patient-facing safety text, so if (c) does bite, an IFU pointer on the panel is normally the proportionate fix. I am not going to infer a risk from the device category and flag the copy for omitting it.

## An inconsistency worth resolving before print

You describe the device as **Class IIb**. A coronary stent incorporating sirolimus as an integral component raises a classification question I cannot answer from the files this skill verifies — MDR Annex VIII classification rules are not in `references/`, and I will not state a rule I cannot cite. **[verify]** with your regulatory lead and against the certificate itself.

It matters commercially, not just formally: if the class stated anywhere on the stand, the leave-behinds, or the panel does not match the certificate, that is a UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] exposure about the goods' authorisation status — the same provision as the "Approved" finding above, and an interventional-cardiology audience is exactly the audience that reads the class off a panel.

## Paste-ready revision

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent delivers sustained drug release over [X] days across the stented segment. CE-marked, available now.

German draft, for native review before use:

> Unser Sirolimus-freisetzender Stent ermöglicht eine kontinuierliche Wirkstofffreisetzung über [X] Tage im gestenteten Segment. CE-gekennzeichnet, ab sofort verfügbar.

Do not render "CE-marked" as "zugelassen".

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "across the full lesion" | Elution uniformity along stent length; available length matrix | R&D / technical file owner |
| "sustained drug release" | Release period from the technical documentation, to fill [X] | R&D |
| "available now" | DE availability on congress dates; certificate scope covers all displayed sizes | Supply chain + RA |
| Class IIb | Class as stated on the certificate | RA / notified body correspondence |
| — | Intended purpose as assessed, verbatim from DoC | RA — unblocks limb (d) |
| — | IFU limitations/contraindications section | RA — settles limb (c) |

## Audience note

I have taken Fachkreise as given, so HWG § 11 is out of scope. If this artwork is reused on an ungated web page, in a press pack, or anywhere a non-professional reader reaches it, § 11 re-engages for devices at nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 only [verified], and the panel needs a second pass.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 3(a) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) scoping sentence for devices — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, no. 4 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- MDR Annex VIII classification rules — **not verified by this skill** [verify]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.evidence:
## First, a premise check

You've described this as **Class IIb**. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent is almost certainly **Class III** under MDR Annex VIII Rule 14 (device incorporating, as an integral part, a substance that would be a medicinal product and acts ancillary to the device) — and separately Rule 8 as a long-term active-substance implant. That doesn't change the wording fixes below, but it does change which technical file, NB certificate and claim-substantiation dossier you point to if a competitor or a Wettbewerbszentrale complaint lands. Worth confirming with RA before the congress, and worth checking no booth material says "Class IIb."

## Verdict on the copy

Not releasable as written. Two blocking issues, two that need filling in.

**Blocker — "Approved"**
There is no *Zulassung* for a medical device. In Germany "zugelassen"/"approved" is read as authority approval of safety and efficacy (the Arzneimittel concept), and applying it to a CE-marked device is the standard example of a misleading claim under **HWG § 3** and **UWG § 5**, and under **MDR Art. 7** (creating a false impression as to the regulatory status). Notified body involvement is a conformity assessment, not an endorsement — you also can't frame the NB as having vouched for the device.
→ Use: "CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745" / "CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745." The NB number belongs next to the CE mark on the label, not as a selling point.

**Blocker — "across the full lesion"**
This is a performance *and* indication claim in one phrase, and it overreaches on both axes:
- It implies coverage of any lesion length, whereas your IFU specifies a lesion-length and reference-vessel-diameter range. Under **MDR Art. 7(d)** you cannot suggest uses beyond the intended purpose that was conformity-assessed — and this phrasing invites use in long/diffuse disease.
- "Drug release across the lesion" conflates elution from the stent with drug distribution in the vessel wall. If you don't have tissue-PK data supporting uniform distribution, the claim isn't substantiated (**MDR Art. 7(a)**, **HWG § 3**).
→ Say what you can prove: the available length matrix, or "uniform drug distribution along the stent length" *if* you have the data.

**Needs substantiation — "sustained drug release"**
Defensible in principle, meaningless as written. Give the release profile actually in the technical documentation (e.g. "≈80 % of sirolimus released over 30 days"). If you support it with a publication at the booth, **HWG § 6** requires the full citation — author, publication, date — visible with the claim, not just in a folder under the counter.

**Missing — intended purpose and risk information**
**MDR Art. 7(c)** prohibits a claim that omits likely risk. For a DES aimed at interventional cardiologists, promotion with no intended purpose, no contraindications and no reference to the antiplatelet regimen is thin. Add the intended purpose verbatim from the IFU and a standing "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten" line.

**Minor — "available now"**
Fine if it is true for Germany specifically on the day, with German-language IFU and UDI/EUDAMED registration in place. If any size in the matrix is backordered or not yet released in DE, drop it. Don't let it be heard as a reimbursement statement.

## Suggested replacement

> **[Produktname] – Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage aus [Polymer/Trägersystem].
> Verfügbar in Durchmessern [A–B] mm und Längen [C–D] mm.
> Zweckbestimmung: [wörtlich aus der Gebrauchsanweisung].
> CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745.
> Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Anforderungen an die duale Thrombozytenaggregationshemmung entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung.
> **Nur für Fachkreise.**

English booth version, same structure: "Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days. CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Available in Germany in [sizes]. Please consult the Instructions for Use for the full intended purpose, contraindications, warnings and antiplatelet therapy requirements. For healthcare professionals only."

## Booth-level items beyond the copy

- **Fachkreise gating.** Congresses often admit press and industry guests. Keep the Fachkreise marking on every panel and handout, and don't leave material in publicly accessible areas — the claims above are only defensible to professionals.
- **German language.** The IFU accompanying product supplied in Germany must be in German. Promotional material can be English for a professional audience, but have German versions of the core claims available.
- **§ 7 HWG / § 299a–b StGB / MedTech Europe Code.** Giveaways, hospitality and any travel or attendance support are the highest-risk part of a congress booth, well above the copy. Brief the stand team on what they can hand over and what they can pay for.
- **Claim substantiation file.** Have the elution data, size matrix and IFU extract ready to produce per claim. Under MDR Art. 7 the burden sits with you.

I'm flagging this from the regulation and standard German promotional practice; get your RA and legal function to sign off the final panel, particularly the classification point.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't run this as written. Two of the three claims are non-compliant, and the stated device class doesn't match the product description — that last point needs resolving before you can even identify the correct substantiation basis.

---

## 1. "Approved" — highest risk, straightforward fix

CE marking is not an approval. For a device, the manufacturer issues a Declaration of Conformity; the notified body issues a certificate. There is no BfArM or EMA "Zulassung," and "approved"/"zugelassen" reads to a German audience as marketing-authorisation language borrowed from pharma — which is exactly the confusion the law targets.

- **MDR Art. 7(a)/(b)** — ascribing properties the device doesn't have / creating a false impression.
- **MDR Art. 20** — prohibits markings and inscriptions likely to mislead as to the meaning of the CE marking.
- **UWG Annex ("Blacklist") No. 4** — per se unfair to state untruthfully that a product has been *bestätigt, gebilligt oder genehmigt* by a public or private body. This is a blacklist item: no balancing test, no de minimis. It's also the cleanest hook for a competitor *Abmahnung*, which is the realistic enforcement path here, not an authority.

**Fix:** "CE marked" / "CE-gekennzeichnet." And do not add the notified body's name, logo, or ID number as an endorsement — the NB number belongs next to the CE mark on the device labelling, not in a booth claim; most NB contracts prohibit promotional use outright.

## 2. "across the full lesion" — unsubstantiated and arguably off-label

Three separate problems in five words:

- **It conflates two things.** "Sustained drug release" is elution kinetics over *time*; "across the full lesion" is drug distribution over *space*. The copy silently merges them into a claim you almost certainly cannot evidence as stated.
- **"Full lesion" is unqualified.** Lesion coverage is a function of stent length selection and your available size matrix. As written it implies coverage of any lesion — including lengths your matrix doesn't reach. That edges into **MDR Art. 7(d)** (suggesting uses outside the intended purpose assessed in conformity assessment).
- **"Delivers" is absolute.** **HWG § 3 S. 2 Nr. 2 lit. a** — false impression that success can be expected with certainty. Also **HWG § 3 S. 2 Nr. 1** if efficacy is ascribed beyond what's held.

**Fix:** quantify and cite. Release duration in days with the data source; coverage expressed as the labelled diameter/length range.

## 3. Missing risk information

**MDR Art. 7(c)** makes it a claims violation to *fail* to inform of a likely risk associated with intended use. For a DES, the obvious ones are stent thrombosis, restenosis, and the mandatory antiplatelet regimen. A booth panel promoting a DES with zero reference to DAPT or to the IFU is exposed here, and under **UWG § 5a** (withholding material information) as well.

Note that HWG § 4 *Pflichtangaben* do not apply to devices — that obligation is pharma-only. But Art. 7(c) plus a clear IFU pointer is the functional equivalent, and it is what reviewers will look for.

---

## Gating question: the device class is wrong

You've specified Class IIb. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent should be **Class III** under MDR Annex VIII on two independent grounds:

- **Rule 8** — implantable devices are IIb *unless* in direct contact with the heart or central circulatory system, which a coronary stent is → III.
- **Rule 14** — devices incorporating a medicinal substance with ancillary action → III.

This isn't pedantry; it changes the review:

- Class III implantables require a **Summary of Safety and Clinical Performance (MDR Art. 32)**. Every promotional claim must be consistent with the SSCP, and the SSCP is public via Eudamed — so any gap between booth copy and SSCP is trivially discoverable by a competitor.
- **Implant card obligation (Art. 18)** applies.
- The sirolimus component was assessed via **medicines-authority consultation (Annex IX, 5.2)**, which further constrains what you may say about the drug.

So: either the classification in your brief is a slip, or the certificate you're relying on isn't for this device. Resolve that first. If it's an **MDD legacy device** under the extended Art. 120 transition (as amended by Reg. 2023/607), it's still lawfully CE marked — but you cannot make "significant changes" to design or intended purpose, and claims must stay inside the older certificate's scope, which is often narrower than what marketing assumes.

---

## Two setting-specific checks

**Fachkreise status is a factual claim about the booth, not a label you apply.** HWG § 2 defines Fachkreise; § 11's restrictions fall away only if access is genuinely controlled. Congress halls routinely admit press, industry analysts, and patient-organisation representatives. If your booth sits in an uncontrolled area, you're in Publikumswerbung and § 11 engages. Verify badge control covering your stand, and mark the material "Nur für Fachkreise."

**Language.** English promotional copy to HCPs at an international congress in Germany is accepted practice, and MPDG § 8 permits English IFU for professional-use devices. But the misleading test under MDR Art. 7 and HWG § 3 is assessed from the German addressee's perspective, and your claims must map onto the German-language intended purpose. "Approved" is a case in point — it translates into the reader's head as "zugelassen," which is worse than the English.

---

## Revised copy

**EN:**
> **[Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent**
> Sirolimus release over [X] days.¹ Available in diameters [x–y] mm and lengths [a–b] mm.
> CE marked. Available in Germany.
> Intended purpose, indications, contraindications, warnings and antiplatelet therapy requirements: see Instructions for Use.
> ¹[Data source / study ref.]
> *For healthcare professionals only.*

**DE:**
> **[Brand] Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent**
> Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage.¹ Verfügbar in Durchmessern [x–y] mm und Längen [a–b] mm.
> CE-gekennzeichnet. In Deutschland verfügbar.
> Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise sowie Angaben zur Thrombozytenaggregationshemmung entnehmen Sie der Gebrauchsanweisung.
> ¹[Datenquelle]
> *Nur für Fachkreise.*

---

## Before print

- [ ] Claims traced line-by-line to intended purpose, IFU, SSCP, and CDE/clinical evaluation report
- [ ] Elution-duration figure sourced; state whether in vitro, preclinical, or clinical — don't leave it ambiguous
- [ ] "Available now" confirmed true for Germany across the advertised size matrix on the congress dates. If any sizes are backordered, either drop the matrix or qualify it
- [ ] No notified body name, number, or logo anywhere in promotional material
- [ ] Correct device class confirmed against the actual certificate
- [ ] Booth access control confirmed as Fachkreise-only
- [ ] Booth hospitality and giveaways checked against MedTech Europe Code / BVMed Kodex Medizinprodukte and **§§ 299a/b StGB** — unrelated to the copy, but it's the other thing that reliably goes wrong at a congress stand

Two things I'd flag as assumptions rather than findings: I've read "Approved and available now" as a Germany-specific availability claim, and I've assumed no comparative intent behind "sustained." If "sustained" is meant to imply an advantage over another DES, that's a comparative claim under UWG § 6 and needs head-to-head data — tell me and I'll review it on that basis instead.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Compliance review — DES booth panel, Germany (Fachkreise)

Not legal advice; based only on the description given. Two of the findings are launch-blocking.

---

### 🔴 1. "Approved" is the wrong legal concept — and misleading in Germany

EU devices are not *approved*. They undergo conformity assessment and carry a CE mark with the notified body's four-digit number. In German, **"zugelassen"** carries the connotation of an authority-granted *Arzneimittel-Zulassung* (efficacy/safety reviewed by BfArM/EMA). Applying it to a device tells cardiologists something about the evidentiary pedigree that isn't true.

Exposure: **MDR Art. 7(b)** (false impression as to properties), **MDR Art. 20(4)** (marks/inscriptions likely to mislead as to the meaning of the CE marking), **§ 3 HWG**, **§ 5 UWG** via **§ 3a UWG**. In practice the realistic enforcement path in Germany is a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sending an Abmahnung — fast, cheap for them, and a congress booth is a visible target.

**Fix:** "CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745" / "CE-Kennzeichnung nach Verordnung (EU) 2017/745." Do **not** upgrade this to "approved by Notified Body ####" — naming the NB as an endorsement is its own Art. 20(4) problem. The NB number belongs next to the CE mark on the label, not in a headline.

### 🔴 2. "Across the full lesion" is an unbounded performance claim

This reads as: the stent covers the lesion, whatever its length. It cannot be true outside your labelled length matrix, and it brushes against **MDR Art. 7(d)** — suggesting uses beyond the intended purpose for which conformity assessment was carried out. It also implicitly denies geographic miss and edge effects, which interventional cardiologists will read as either naïve or a superiority claim.

**Fix:** bound it to the labelled range and to correct sizing — "lengths [a]–[b] mm; single-stent coverage for lesions up to [Y] mm when sized per IFU."

### 🟠 3. "Sustained drug release" is unquantified and unsourced

Under **MDR Art. 7(a)** and **Annex I Section 23**, and **§ 3 Satz 2 Nr. 1 HWG**, a performance claim must correspond to the intended purpose and be backed by the clinical evaluation. "Sustained" states no duration, no release profile, no data. To a Fachkreis audience it also carries an implicit comparative ("more sustained than what?"), which pulls in **§ 6 UWG** — comparative advertising must be objective, verifiable and like-for-like.

**Fix:** give the number and the source — "controlled sirolimus release over [X] days (PK/elution data, [reference])." If any comparison is intended, make it explicit and head-to-head, or drop it.

Note additionally: because the sirolimus is an ancillary medicinal substance, the NB obtained a scientific opinion on it from a competent authority or EMA (**Annex IX Section 5.2**). Claims about the drug component must stay inside what that opinion and your intended purpose actually cover.

### 🟠 4. No risk information at all

**MDR Art. 7(c)** prohibits claims that fail to inform of a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose. A bare efficacy statement on a DES — with no mention of stent thrombosis, restenosis, DAPT requirements, or contraindications, and no pointer to the IFU — is the textbook Art. 7(c) exposure. A short IFU reference line resolves it.

### 🟡 5. "Available now" — verify, then date it

Permissible only if the device is genuinely placed on the German market at the time of the congress. Pre-launch "available now" is straightforwardly misleading (§ 5 UWG, § 3 HWG). If any size, configuration or non-CE prototype is shown on the stand that isn't yet conformant, **MDR Art. 21** requires a visible sign stating it is for presentation/demonstration only and cannot be made available until brought into compliance.

### 🟡 6. Fachkreise scoping

Mark the panel and all handouts **"Nur für Fachkreise"** and control access. Congress halls leak — press, industry guests, patient-org representatives. Once laypersons are the realistic audience, **§ 11 HWG** constraints apply and the analysis changes. The same applies if the panel is photographed onto LinkedIn or the company website, which is where most of these cases actually originate.

Also confirm the German-language position for anything functioning as device information rather than pure advertising (MPDG language rules; English is generally workable toward professional users, but worth a documented decision).

---

### ⚠️ Separate flag: the stated classification looks wrong

You describe this as **Class IIb**. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent should be **Class III** under MDR Annex VIII on two independent grounds:

- **Rule 8** — implantable, and in direct contact with the central circulatory system; the MDR's definition of that term expressly lists the *arteriae coronariae*.
- **Rule 14** — incorporates an integral medicinal substance with ancillary action.

If "IIb" is just shorthand in your brief, ignore this. If it reflects the actual technical documentation, it's a conformity-route problem far larger than the copy, and it should not appear in any customer-facing or partner material. Worth confirming against the CE certificate before the congress.

---

### Suggested rewrite

**EN**
> **[Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent system**
> Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days.¹ Available in lengths [a]–[b] mm for single-stent coverage of lesions up to [Y] mm when sized per IFU.
> ¹[Data source: study, n, endpoint, timepoint]
> CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Available in Germany from [date].
> Intended purpose, indications, contraindications, warnings and residual risks: see Instructions for Use.
> *For healthcare professionals only.*

**DE**
> **[Marke] Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage.¹ Stentlängen [a]–[b] mm zur Versorgung von Läsionen bis [Y] mm mit einem Stent bei Sizing gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.
> ¹[Datenquelle]
> CE-Kennzeichnung nach Verordnung (EU) 2017/745. In Deutschland verfügbar ab [Datum].
> Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Restrisiken: siehe Gebrauchsanweisung.
> *Nur für Fachkreise.*

Three inputs still needed from the team before this can go to print: the actual release duration and its data source, the labelled length range, and the confirmed German availability date.

# Device Claims Review: "Surgeons love it" headline pair

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Reusable surgical retractor — Class I
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 0 substantiate, 2 OK — both carry a `Verify`.

This is subjective preference copy with no clinical, performance, or certification content. It makes no therapeutic claim, ascribes no function, and stays inside the assessed intended purpose. I identified **no breaches** on the material supplied. The two open items below are questions for the file, not findings.

**Ready to publish:** see the gate at the end — I can't clear copy for publication.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A general sentiment claim with no therapeutic effect ascribed (HWG § 3 no. 1 not engaged) and no function or property asserted (MDR Art. 7(a)/(b) not engaged). It is unverifiable preference language, not a statement about the device's Zwecktauglichkeit or expected results.
**Evidence needed:** None as it stands. But see `Also engaged`.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Ergebnisse … von **Tests**", "wesentliche Merkmale") — **if** this line is anywhere presented as resting on data: a user survey, a clinical evaluation user-feedback section, a trade-show poll, an NPS figure. The moment sentiment is sourced to a study, the study's scope and representativeness become the claim, and a non-representative or cherry-picked sample is a § 5 problem. Kept out of `Breach:` because nothing you gave me says such data exists. [verified]
**Call:** Verify — confirm the line is *not* paired anywhere (deck, footnote, badge, landing page) with a survey figure or "n=" reference.
**Suggested fix:** None needed if it stays unsourced. If you do have survey data and want to use it, the safer paste-ready form is: `In einer Anwenderbefragung unter [n] Chirurginnen und Chirurgen [Zeitraum] bewerteten [x] % die Handhabung mit „gut" oder „sehr gut".`

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** "Enjoy using" is a handling/preference claim, not a clinical one. MDR Art. 7(d) is not engaged: it suggests no user population, setting, or indication outside "manual retraction of tissue … during open procedures." HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (*Erfolg mit Sicherheit*) is not engaged either — the certainty on offer is about enjoyment, not about a therapeutic Erfolg, which is what no. 2(a) addresses.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6 — "actually" carries an implicit comparison ("unlike the ones you have now"). § 6(1) only bites where a **Mitbewerber erkennbar** is made. Against the retractor category at large, no competitor is identifiable and § 6 does not engage. It would engage **if** this line runs adjacent to a named or visually identifiable competitor product, or in a placement where the German market can tell which incumbent is meant — then the comparison must clear every limb of § 6(2), and "enjoyable" fails no. 2 as non-objective and non-*nachprüfbar*. Condition: check the placement, not the sentence. [verified]
**Call:** Verify — confirm the surrounding layout names or shows no competitor.
**Suggested fix:** None required as standalone copy.

## Open questions (not findings)

**Limb (c) — risk omission.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this material. A reusable device also carries reprocessing conditions that live in the IFU. I'm not flagging either, because I haven't seen the IFU and inferring a risk from the device category would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking the IFU; where (c) genuinely bites on trade copy this short, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix, not safety text.

**Limb (d) — images.** I reviewed text only. The intended purpose is limited to **open procedures**. Any accompanying photography, illustration, or caption showing a minimally invasive, endoscopic, or laparoscopic setting would breach Art. 7(d) regardless of the headline being clean — and that breach is cured by changing the image or extending the conformity assessment, not by adding evidence. Send me the visuals and I'll cover them.

**Drafting note (no provision engaged):** for German hospital procurement, two lines of subjective preference give a Vergabe process nothing to score. That's a commercial observation, not a compliance one.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Confirmation the line is not sourced to a survey/poll anywhere in the campaign; if it is, the raw sample size, period and question wording | Marketing / product management |
| "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using." | Final layout showing no competitor named or depicted alongside | Marketing / agency |
| Whole asset | IFU: any likely risk or limitation for use in line with the intended purpose | Regulatory affairs |
| Accompanying visuals | All campaign imagery and captions, for an Art. 7(d) pass against "open procedures" | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11 — `references/hwg.md`; **not applicable**, audience is Fachkreise [verified]
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

One thing I deliberately did **not** raise: HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (*Äußerungen Dritter*) against "Surgeons love it." § 11 applies only outside Fachkreise, and your audience is hospital procurement. If this copy is ever repurposed onto an ungated public page, that changes — and note that even then, no. 11 catches testimonials only where they are missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend, not testimonials as such.

## Before answering "Ready to publish"

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis. Here's the one-page brief to take to counsel:

- **Asset:** two-line headline pair, Fachkreise, German market, Class I reusable retractor
- **Claims cleared:** "Surgeons love it." / "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using." — no therapeutic claim, no function ascribed, no intended-purpose drift, no certification claim
- **Provisions checked:** MDR Art. 7(a)–(d); HWG § 3, § 11 (inapplicable); UWG § 5, § 6
- **Open questions:** (1) IFU risk content vs. Art. 7(c); (2) campaign imagery vs. Art. 7(d) "open procedures"; (3) whether "Surgeons love it" is sourced to data anywhere
- **The three things to ask counsel:** Does unsourced sentiment puffery of this kind survive § 5(1) in the Fachkreise context here? Does "actually" become § 6 comparative advertising in your planned placements? Does the IFU contain a limitation that must travel with promotional material?

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Device Claims Review: headline copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Surgical retractor, reusable — Class I (no notified body involvement assumed for Class I non-sterile/non-measuring; confirm)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — as stated by you. See the gating note under Open questions.
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 2 verify, 0 OK-as-final.

**No breaches identified** against MDR Art. 7(a)–(d), HWG § 3, or UWG §§ 5/6 on the material supplied. This is short preference-and-experience copy that makes no clinical, performance or certification claim, so most of the statutory surface simply isn't engaged. What's left is substantiation basis and campaign context.

**Ready to publish:** see the gate at the end — I can't clear it, but there's nothing here I'd hold it for.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Ascribes no function or property (Art. 7(a)), creates no impression about treatment or diagnosis (Art. 7(b)), suggests no use outside "manual retraction of tissue … during open procedures" (Art. 7(d)), and attributes no therapeutic effect (HWG § 3 no. 1). It is a statement about user preference, not about what the device does.
**Evidence needed:** Nothing, if it stays as an unquantified preference line. If the campaign anywhere attaches a number, a survey, a user count or a quoted user to it, the line becomes an Angabe über wesentliche Merkmale under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 and needs the underlying data on file.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if "love it" is presented as, or sits next to, survey/evaluation data that doesn't support it, or data drawn from a different user group than "surgeons".
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 — only if the audience is in fact Publikum (see Open questions). Even then, third-party statements are prohibited for devices only where missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend; a generic "surgeons love it" with no fabricated or distorted endorsement behind it is not automatically caught.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) — if the line evolves into claims about the manufacturer's standing or track record ("the choice of Germany's leading surgeons").
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** None required. If you want the line to be cheap to defend rather than merely defensible, anchor it: `"Von Chirurginnen und Chirurgen in [N] Kliniken im Routineeinsatz."` — verifiable and narrow.

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) prohibits falsely creating the impression that "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". The promised "Erfolg" here is the reader's handling experience, not a therapeutic or diagnostic outcome, so the guarantee limb isn't reached on this wording. No harmful-effects reassurance, so § 3 no. 2(b) isn't reached either. Nothing in "enjoy using" suggests a use outside the assessed intended purpose (Art. 7(d)).
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the line as written.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 6(2) no. 2 — "actually" carries an implied contrast with other retractors. § 6 bites only where a Mitbewerber is **erkennbar** under § 6(1). Against the anonymous whole field, no competitor is identified; but if this headline runs beside a named competitor, a comparison table, or a visual that makes the incumbent recognisable, it becomes comparative advertising — and "enjoyable to use" is not an objective, nachprüfbar, typical characteristic, so it would fail no. 2. Fix in that context: replace with a measurable handling property (Gewicht, Griffgeometrie, Anzahl Reprozessierungszyklen).
- MDR Art. 7(a)/(b) and HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — if the campaign chains the enjoyment claim to a clinical consequence ("enjoy using it — and get better exposure / shorter procedures / fewer complications"). Ergonomics-to-outcome bridges are where this kind of copy usually breaks, and that bridge would need data.
**Call:** Verify (context, not substance)

## Open questions

**The Fachkreise designation is doing real work here — confirm the channel, not just the intent.** You've told me the audience is hospital procurement, and I've reviewed on that basis. But an ungated web page or brochure PDF that anyone can reach is not Fachkreise merely because the buyer is. If this copy sits anywhere public, HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 come into scope. Practically, the exposure even then looks modest: no. 7 needs health-impairment-by-non-use or health-improvement-by-use framing, and this copy makes no health claim at all; no. 11 would put "Surgeons love it" under the missbräuchlich/abstoßend/irreführend test rather than banning it. So the designation changes the analysis without, on this wording, changing the outcome — but confirm it before you reuse the line on copy that does make claims.

**Limb (c) — I can't resolve it from what I have.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from the intended purpose alone whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with in-purpose use that belongs in advertising — for a *reusable* instrument, reprocessing constraints (validated cycles, inspection before reuse) are the usual candidate. Worth checking against the IFU. Note the proportionality point: a two-line headline isn't expected to carry safety text, and where (c) genuinely bites on short-form copy, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix rather than a rewrite.

**Check the accompanying imagery against limb (d) before this goes out.** The intended purpose is confined to **open** procedures and manual retraction. A visual of laparoscopic or minimally invasive use, a self-retaining configuration, or a non-surgical setting would breach Art. 7(d) even though the words don't — and (d) is not curable by evidence. It's cured by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment.

## Drafting note (not a finding)

For hospital procurement, this copy says nothing procurable. It carries no purpose statement, no reprocessing data, no materials, no instrument dimensions — nothing a Einkauf or ZSVA reviewer scores against. That's a commercial weakness, not a legal one, but the low-risk version is also the more persuasive one for this audience. Paste-ready alternative, if useful:

> **Wiederverwendbarer Wundhaken für die manuelle Gewebsretraktion in der offenen Chirurgie.**
> Ergonomischer Griff, [N] validierte Reprozessierungszyklen, [Material]. Im Routineeinsatz in [N] Kliniken.

Bracketed figures need substantiation on file before use (UWG § 5(2) no. 1).

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Any user-feedback, evaluation or survey basis, if the line is ever quantified or attributed | Marketing / clinical affairs |
| "you'll actually enjoy using" | Confirmation of surrounding campaign context — no named/recognisable competitor, no ergonomics-to-clinical-outcome bridge | Marketing |
| Whole asset | Confirmation the channel is gated to Fachkreise | Marketing / digital |
| Whole asset | IFU check for a likely risk on in-purpose use (reprocessing limits) | Regulatory / QM |
| Accompanying imagery | Depicts open-procedure manual retraction only | Marketing / regulatory |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 2(a), no. 2(b), no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 (devices: only nos. 7–9, 11, 12 apply) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis. In particular, whether "Surgeons love it" and "you'll actually enjoy using" read as non-actionable puffery or as substantiable Angaben is a line drawn by German case law, which this review does not cover, and I won't characterise that line for you.

  2. Does "actually" make a Mitbewerber erkennbar under UWG § 6(1) in this market, given the competitive field for surgical retractors?
  3. Is the intended distribution channel sufficient to keep this outside HWG § 11 as Fachkreisewerbung?
