# Device Claims Review: retractor tagline

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Reusable surgical retractor — Class I (self-certified; no notified body indicated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 clean as written.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The good news first: this copy makes no performance claim, no clinical-benefit claim, and no claim about certification. **Limb (d) clears** — nothing here suggests laparoscopic/MIS use, a new user population, or a setting outside open procedures. That is the limb that most often bites, and it doesn't here. The exposure is narrower than a generic marketing review would suggest: substantiation of one sentence, and one word.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** It ascribes no therapeutic effect (HWG § 3 no. 1 not engaged), no function or property the device lacks (Art. 7(a)), and no treatment or diagnostic impression (Art. 7(b)). It is a statement about user sentiment, not about what the device does.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "wesentliche Merkmale" — **if** the sentence is read as an assertion of measured user acceptance rather than as reklamehafte Anpreisung. Surgeon acceptance is a real driver of a procurement decision, so the § 5(1) materiality filter ("geeignet, den [...] Marktteilnehmer zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen") is plausibly met for this audience. Which reading applies turns on the puffery/factual-assertion line, which is case law this skill does not verify — I won't tell you how that would come out.
**Evidence needed:** A user-acceptance survey or handling evaluation — sample size, sites, date, question wording. If one exists, cite the figure instead of the adjective; a cited figure moves the claim out of § 5(2) no. 1 territory entirely and is cheap to defend. If none exists, this sentence is carrying risk for no benefit.
**Call:** Needs substantiation (or replace)

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually **enjoy** using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Handling comfort is not a therapeutic Erfolg, so HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (*Erfolg mit Sicherheit*) is not engaged despite the definite future tense — the copy promises no clinical outcome at all. No Art. 7 limb reaches subjective user experience here.
**Also engaged:** **UWG § 6** — this is the sharpest item in the asset, and it hangs on one word. "**Actually**" asserts a contrast: other retractors are not enjoyable to use. § 6(1) is satisfied where a Mitbewerber is made recognisable "unmittelbar oder mittelbar" — no naming required. Across the whole retractor category, no single competitor is identifiable and § 6 likely stays out. But it comes in if **any** of these are true of the full asset: a competitor is named, shown, or pictured alongside; the surrounding copy narrows the contrast ("unlike the [X]-style retractors"); or the specific retractor sub-segment is concentrated enough that the market reads it as one incumbent. If § 6(1) is engaged, § 6(2) no. 2 is hard to clear — "enjoyment" is not an **objektiv, nachprüfbar** characteristic, and that limb fails even where the underlying sentiment is accurate.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — not curable by evidence. Cured by deleting "actually," which costs the line nothing.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

Two versions, depending on whether the survey exists.

**If you have acceptance data** (replace the bracketed values with the real ones):

> In der Anwenderbewertung 2026 bewerteten [94] % von [120] Chirurgen an [18] Kliniken die Handhabung mit gut oder sehr gut. Ergonomischer, ausbalancierter Retraktor zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Exposition des OP-Situs bei offenen Eingriffen. [Methodik und vollständige Ergebnisse: Link]

EN: *In our 2026 handling evaluation, [94]% of [120] surgeons at [18] hospitals rated handling good or very good. An ergonomic, balanced retractor for manual tissue retraction to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures. [Method and full results: link]*

**If you do not have data** — drop the sentiment claim and sell a verifiable property instead:

> Ergonomischer Griff, ausbalanciert für lange offene Eingriffe. Zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Exposition des OP-Situs.

EN: *Ergonomic grip, balanced for long open procedures. For manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure.*

Both versions track the assessed intended purpose verbatim, which keeps limb (d) clean, and neither contains a comparison.

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation, and it is benefit-framed throughout. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in customer-facing material. I'm deliberately not inferring one from "it's a retractor" — that would make the finding unfalsifiable, since every benefit-framed ad omits some inferable risk.

Worth checking against the IFU. Note the proportionality point: for a 12-word tagline aimed at procurement, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix if (c) genuinely bites — not safety text in the headline.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it" | User-acceptance survey: N, sites, date, question wording, full results | Marketing / clinical affairs |
| "actually enjoy using" | The full asset — does anything name, show or narrow to a competitor? | Marketing |
| (c) omission | Does the IFU record a likely risk in normal use? | Regulatory / technical documentation |
| Audience gating | Is this page/asset access-restricted to Fachkreise, or publicly readable? | Marketing / web |

On the last row: you've told me Fachkreise, and I've reviewed on that basis, so § 11 is out. But a B2B page anyone can open is not automatically Fachkreise. If this tagline ends up on an ungated public page, § 11 comes into scope — and the item to look at then is no. 11 (*Äußerungen Dritter*), though note it bites only where the third-party statement is missbräuchlich, abstoßend **or irreführend**. "Surgeons love it" is not a quoted testimonial and would only reach no. 11 through the misleading limb, which loops back to the substantiation question above.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (scope note only; not applied) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

One drafting note outside the legal analysis, offered as such: this tagline tells a procurement reader nothing about the device — no material, no reprocessing cycles, no blade geometry, no sterilisation profile. For a *reusable* Class I instrument sold to hospital procurement, total cost of ownership and reprocessing validation are usually the decision drivers, and the compliant rewrites above are also the stronger sales copy for that reader.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not usable as written. Both sentences are claims, neither is substantiable, and one of them becomes flatly illegal the moment the copy escapes a Fachkreise gate. It also gives a procurement reader nothing to procure on.

---

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated third-party endorsement**

This is a testimonial claim, not puffery, because it asserts a fact about real clinicians' preference.

- **MDR Art. 7** prohibits text that creates a false impression regarding performance. An aggregate preference claim with no source does exactly that.
- **§ 6 HWG** applies to Fachkreise *and* Publikum alike: if you reference expert statements or testimonials, you must give the author's name, their professional position, and the date of the statement, and quote accurately. "Surgeons" as an anonymous collective fails all three.
- **§ 3 HWG / § 5 UWG**: health-sector advertising runs under the Strengeprinzip — the burden of proof is on you, and "love" has no measurable referent, so the burden can't be discharged. In practice this gets enforced by a competitor Abmahnung, not by an authority.

**2. The Fachkreise gate is load-bearing, and "Fachkreise" needs to be real**

If this sits on an open product page or an ungated PDF, it is Publikumswerbung, and **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 HWG** bans advertising a Gegenstand with claims that it is professionally recommended, tested, or used — full stop. No amount of survey data rescues it there.

Gating means an actual mechanism (login, DocCheck, Fachkreis-Bestätigung), not a "Nur für Fachkreise" line in the footer. Worth noting: hospital procurement staff *do* qualify under **§ 2 HWG**, but via the "Einrichtungen, die der Gesundheit dienen" route — not because they're Heilberufsangehörige. That distinction matters if you ever gate by professional credential.

**3. "you'll actually enjoy using" — implicit comparative disparagement**

"Actually" presupposes that the retractors they use today are unpleasant. That's a comparison against unnamed competitors. **§ 6 Abs. 2 UWG** requires comparisons to be objective, verifiable, and tied to relevant characteristics, and prohibits disparagement. An implied "unlike everything else on your tray" is neither objective nor verifiable.

**4. The claim sits outside the Zweckbestimmung**

Intended purpose is retraction and exposure maintenance. Enjoyment is not a performance attribute of that purpose. If the real differentiator is grip ergonomics — say so, and note that an ergonomics claim is a usability claim, which needs a **IEC 62366-1** usability engineering file / handling evaluation behind it, not user enthusiasm.

**5. Nothing here supports a procurement decision**

This audience buys on: steel grade, blade sizes and variants, validated reprocessing (cycle count, ISO 17664 instructions, validation to ISO 15883 / EN 285), tray and set compatibility, UDI-DI, lifecycle cost, availability.

One Class I–specific point they *will* check: as a **reusable surgical instrument this is Class Ir**, so Notified Body involvement is required under **MDR Art. 52(7)(c)** and the CE mark carries an NB number. Show it. Equally, don't let marketing upgrade that into "Notified Body certified" in general — the NB's scope is limited to reprocessing and related safety aspects.

**6. Language**

German market, German copy. Labelling and IFU must be German under MPDG/MPBetreibV regardless; English marketing to a German hospital reads as an incomplete dossier even where it's permitted.

---

## Rewrite

**Option A — drop the endorsement angle (recommended)**

> **Sichere Exposition. Zyklus für Zyklus.**
> Wundhaken zur manuellen Gewebsretraktion zur Aufrechterhaltung der Situsexposition bei offenen Eingriffen. Edelstahl [1.4301], [n] Blattgrößen, validierte Aufbereitung über [n] Zyklen nach ISO 17664.

**Option B — keep a preference claim, made lawful**

> In einer Anwenderbefragung unter [n] Chirurginnen und Chirurgen an [x] Kliniken ([MM/JJJJ]) bewerteten [n] % die Griffergonomie mit „gut" oder „sehr gut". [Quellenangabe]

Option B is only viable behind a genuine Fachkreise gate, and only if the survey actually exists with methodology, n, date, and sample documented.

Footer either way: manufacturer, product name, "Medizinprodukt", CE + NB number, Fachkreise designation, copy revision date.

---

## To close this out I'd need

1. Channel — gated web, print brochure, Messestand, or tender document? Determines whether § 11 HWG is in play at all.
2. Does a user survey exist? If yes, send methodology and I'll tell you what's quotable.
3. What is the actual ergonomic differentiator — grip geometry, weight, surface finish? That's the claim worth building, and it's substantiable.

Keep the substantiation for every retained claim in a claims dossier under your QMS (ISO 13485 §7.2 / MDR Art. 7) — that file is what an Abmahnung gets answered with. Regulatory Affairs and German competition counsel should sign off before release; this is a copy review, not a legal opinion.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The copy is not usable as-is. Not because it's illegal on its face, but because the one substantive claim it makes ("Surgeons love it") is an unsubstantiated factual assertion in a health-advertising context, and everything else in it is register-wrong for German hospital procurement. It also tells a procurement buyer nothing they need in order to buy.

---

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated collective endorsement claim (highest risk)**

German courts apply the *Strengeprinzip* to health-related advertising: heightened requirements for accuracy, clarity and unambiguity, with the burden on the advertiser. A statement about what a professional group collectively thinks reads as a verifiable *Tatsachenbehauptung*, not as *reklamehafte Anpreisung* — especially before a Fachkreis audience, which parses it as an evidence claim. Without survey data behind it: **§ 3 HWG** (irreführende Werbung — applies to all audiences, not just laypersons) and **§ 5 UWG**.

If you *do* have data, the fix creates a second obligation: **§ 6 HWG** requires an exact *Fundstelle* when advertising with expert opinions, testimonials or professional publications, and the citation must be accurate and representative.

Note a common misconception here — **§ 4 HWG** *Pflichtangaben* apply to Arzneimittel, not Medizinprodukte. You do not need a mandatory-information block. Don't over-comply on that axis.

**2. "you'll actually enjoy using" — implied ergonomics claim + implied category disparagement**

Two problems in four words:

- *"enjoy using"* is a usability/ergonomics performance claim by implication. **MDR Art. 7** prohibits ascribing functions or properties the device does not have. If you want a handling advantage, back it with usability engineering output (**IEC 62366-1**) or a comparative handling study.
- *"actually"* presupposes that competing retractors are unpleasant. That is a blanket comparative jab at unnamed competitors — **§ 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 5 UWG** (*pauschale Herabsetzung*). In a market as narrow as surgical retractors, "identifiable competitor" is easier to establish than you'd expect. Moderate risk, cheap to remove.

**3. Register and address form**

`you'll` translated straight into German gives you either *du* (impossible for Klinikeinkauf) or a consumer-magazine *Sie*. Neither lands. German B2B medtech copy for procurement is declarative and specification-led; emotive lifestyle framing reads as a credibility signal *against* the product. Also use *Chirurginnen und Chirurgen* rather than the generic masculine.

**4. Channel determines which rule set applies**

*Fachkreise* under **§ 2 HWG** covers hospital procurement. But the Fachkreis restriction has to be technically enforced — access control, DocCheck or equivalent. Copy sitting on an open website is treated as public advertising regardless of who you intended to reach, which pulls in **§ 11 Abs. 1 HWG**. For Medizinprodukte only a subset of § 11 Abs. 1 applies (the statute limits it by cross-reference), so the "ärztlich empfohlen" prohibition in Nr. 2 does not catch devices — but Nr. 11 (*Äußerungen Dritter*, where misleading) does. Worth having your Rechtsabteilung confirm the current cross-reference against the statute text; my point stands either way, because § 3 HWG and § 5 UWG bind you in front of Fachkreise too.

**5. Classification detail that affects your CE mark artwork**

"Retracting" is named explicitly in the **MDR Art. 2(19)** definition of *reusable surgical instrument*. Under Rule 6 that lands you in Class I, but as **Class Ir** — **Art. 52(7)(a)** requires notified body involvement for the reprocessing aspects, and the CE mark must therefore carry the four-digit NB number. If your creative shows a bare CE mark, that's wrong. If you make any reprocessing claim, it has to match the validated **ISO 17664** instructions and the validated cycle count.

**6. Nothing here supports a procurement decision**

Missing: material and grade, blade dimensions, weight, validated reprocessing cycles and cycle limit, UDI-DI, lifetime, compatibility with existing sets, price basis.

---

## Rewrites

**If you have no user data** (safest, ship today):

> **Manuelle Gewebsretraktion mit stabiler Situsexposition bei offenen Eingriffen.**
> [Material/Werkstoff], [Gewicht], Blattgrößen [–]. Wiederaufbereitbar, validierte Aufbereitung nach ISO 17664, [n] Zyklen.

**If you have a real survey** (§ 6 HWG-compliant):

> In einer Anwenderbefragung an [n] Kliniken ([Monat/Jahr], Methodik: [–]) bewerteten [x] % der befragten Chirurginnen und Chirurgen die Handhabung als besser als bei ihrem bisher verwendeten Instrument.¹
> ¹ [vollständige Fundstelle]

**If you have one named surgeon willing to be quoted** — attributed testimonials *are* permitted to Fachkreise, which is the real safe harbour your original copy was groping toward:

> „Der Griff liegt auch nach 90 Minuten sicher in der Hand."
> — Dr. med. [Name], Oberärztin [Fachabteilung], [Klinik], [Datum]

The attributed quote does the emotional work the original wanted, and does it legally, because it's a sourced individual opinion rather than an unsourced claim about a profession.

---

## What I'd need to firm this up

Which channel (gated portal vs. open web vs. print trade press vs. Messe), and whether any user-satisfaction or handling data exists — with n, method and date. Those two answers change which of the three rewrites you can use.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship as-is. Nothing here is a hard prohibition given the Fachkreise audience, but the headline is an unsubstantiated factual claim in health-product advertising — the single highest-frequency Abmahnung target in this market — and the copy doesn't speak to the buyer you've named.

## Findings, ranked

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated claim of general professional endorsement (high)**

In German Heilmittelwerbung, courts apply strict proof standards (strenger Wahrheitsbeweis) and the advertiser carries the burden. "Surgeons love it" reads as a statement of fact about broad professional acceptance, not as recognisable puffery — and for a trade audience it will be read as an implicit claim that you have the data. Exposure: § 3 HWG (Irreführung), § 5 UWG, MDR Art. 7.

Fix it one of two ways:
- **Substantiate and attribute**: "In a user evaluation at *n* hospitals, *x* of *y* surgeons rated handling as better than their current instrument" — with method, sample and date disclosable on request, and the underlying data filed in your claims-substantiation documentation (MDR Annex II expects claims to be traceable to evidence).
- **Or drop it.** If it's genuine post-market feedback, individual, real, representative testimonials are permissible toward Fachkreise. Aggregated "surgeons love it" is not the same thing and is much harder to defend.

**2. "actually" — implicit disparagement of unnamed competitors (medium)**

"The retractor you'll *actually* enjoy using" asserts that other retractors are not enjoyable. If any competitor is identifiable — and in a narrow retractor segment that's arguable — this is comparative advertising under § 6 UWG, which requires comparison on objective, verifiable, relevant characteristics. "Enjoyable" is none of those. Even where no competitor is identifiable, § 5 UWG remains in play. Delete the word; it carries all of the legal risk and none of the meaning.

**3. Audience mismatch (medium — commercial, not legal)**

You've specified hospital procurement, but the copy addresses the surgeon ("you'll"). Procurement decides on reprocessing validation and cycle life, material spec, instrument weight and balance, price per use over service life, ISO 13485 status, UDI/GTIN and delivery reliability. "Enjoy" is not a line item in a Vergabe evaluation. Surgeon preference *is* a legitimate input to that decision — but it has to be framed as evidence procurement can cite internally, which loops back to finding 1.

**4. Fachkreis gating (medium, depends on placement)**

The Fachkreise status is what keeps § 11 Abs. 1 HWG (incl. Nr. 2 and Nr. 11, which restrict third-party endorsements and recommendations from health professionals) out of scope — those apply to Publikumswerbung only. That protection evaporates if this sits on an ungated public web page. If the placement is web, put it behind a Fachkreis-Schranke. If it's a printed procurement mailing or trade-fair material, no action needed.

**5. Language (low)**

The copy is English. Advertising itself needn't be German (labelling and IFU must be), and English trade copy is common. But note the tone doesn't transfer: "Chirurgen lieben ihn" lands considerably more aggressively in German and would sharpen finding 1 rather than soften it.

## What's fine

- No Art. 7(d) problem: the copy doesn't suggest any use outside "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
- No Art. 7(a)/(b) problem from "enjoy": it's a usability statement, not a clinical performance or safety claim.
- Class I self-certification isn't a constraint on this copy as such — but it does mean no notified body reviewed your claims, so the substantiation file is entirely your own responsibility.
- No HWG mandatory-information (Pflichtangaben) duty here; that regime is for Arzneimittel.

## Rewrite options

Tone preserved, claims anchored — all placeholders must be replaced with what your validated IFU and technical documentation actually support:

> **Designed for the hand that holds it for three hours.**
> Balanced at [x] g. Fully dismantlable, validated for [n] machine reprocessing cycles per ISO 17664.

> **Sustained exposure, sustained grip.**
> Atraumatic blade geometry, [material spec], [n]-cycle validated service life. Requested by name at [x] hospitals since [year].

That last line is the compliant version of "surgeons love it": a verifiable fact about reorder behaviour rather than an unprovable claim about sentiment.

## To sign this off

Tell me: (a) is there any survey, evaluation or post-market data behind "surgeons love it"; (b) what's the placement — gated web, print, trade fair; (c) your validated reprocessing cycle count and material spec, so the rewrites can be made concrete.

Worth noting this is a copy review against the applicable framework, not legal advice — the substantiation question in finding 1 is one your Regulatory function should countersign before publication.
